mcqs.q: Given AB perpendicular to BC, AD perpendicular to DC, and AB congruent to AD, with AC as common hypotenuse, triangles ABC and ADC are congruent by
mcqs.why: Both triangles are right-angled (at B and D), they share the hypotenuse AC, and one leg pair AB and AD is congruent. Right angle, hypotenuse and one leg give the H.L congruence postulate.

mcqs.q: Rectangle QUAD has diagonals intersecting at C, with QC = x and DC = 3x - 8, where QC and DC are halves of the two diagonals. What is x?
mcqs.why: The diagonals of a rectangle are congruent and bisect each other, so their halves are congruent: QC = DC. Hence x = 3x - 8, so 8 = 3x - x = 2x, giving x = 4.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 10
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A.A.A is not a sufficient condition for congruence: equal angles alone allow different sizes, while A.S.A, H.S (hypotenuse-side) and S.A.A are sufficient.
  • S.A.S is a legitimate congruence condition, but S.S.A and A.A.A are not sufficient conditions for declaring two triangles congruent.
  • The diagonal of a rectangle, a square or a parallelogram divides it into two congruent triangles, but the diagonal of a trapezium does not.
  • In the correspondence triangle ABC congruent to triangle DEF, corresponding parts match in order: angle B corresponds to angle E and side CA corresponds to side FD.
  • If angle A is congruent to angle B in triangle ABC, the bisector of the remaining angle C divides the triangle into two congruent triangles.
  • Any point on the bisector of an angle is equidistant from the arms of the angle, so the meeting point of two angle bisectors in a triangle is equidistant from all three sides.
  • In an isosceles triangle, the segment from the apex to the midpoint of the base bisects the vertex angle and is perpendicular to the base, proved by S.S.S.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Which of the following is not a sufficient condition for the congruency of two triangles?

Options: (a) A.S.A ≅ A.S.A (b) H.S ≅ H.S (c) S.A.A ≅ S.A.A (d) A.A.A ≅ A.A.A

Correct answer: A.A.A ≅ A.A.A

Q: Q1(ii). The diagonal of ________ does not divide it into two congruent triangles.

Options: (a) rectangle (b) square (c) parallelogram (d) trapezium

Correct answer: trapezium

Q: Q1(iii). In a given correspondence of two triangles, if △ABC ≅ △DEF, then which of the following is not correct?

Options: (a) ∠B ≅ ∠E (b) CA ≅ FD (c) ∠CBA ≅ ∠FED (d) ∠ABC ≅ ∠EFD

Correct answer: ∠ABC ≅ ∠EFD

Q: Q1(iv). In △ABC, if ∠A ≅ ∠B then bisector of ________ divides the △ABC into two congruent triangles.

Options: (a) ∠A (b) ∠B (c) ∠C (d) any one of its angles

Correct answer: ∠C

Q: Q1(v). Which of the following is a legitimate reason for declaring two triangles to be congruent?

Options: (a) SSA ≅ SSA (b) SAS ≅ SAS (c) AAA ≅ AAA (d) all of these

Correct answer: SAS ≅ SAS

Q: Q2. In a △PQR, the bisectors of ∠Q and ∠R meet at O. Prove that O is equidistant from the sides of the triangle.

Ans: Given:
In △PQR, QO is the bisector of ∠Q and RO is the bisector of ∠R; the two bisectors meet at the interior point O.
To Prove:
O is equidistant from the three sides of △PQR
Construction:
From O draw OL ⊥ PQ, OM ⊥ QR and ON ⊥ RP.
Proof:
O lies on the bisector of ∠Q — statement (given)
∴ OL ≅ OM — reason: any point on the bisector of an angle is equidistant from its arms
O lies on the bisector of ∠R — statement (given)
∴ OM ≅ ON — reason: any point on the bisector of an angle is equidistant from its arms
∴ OL ≅ OM ≅ ON — reason: transitive property
Hence O is equidistant from the sides of the triangle.
Hence proved.

Q: Q3. In the given figure AB ≅ CB and ∠A ≅ ∠C. Prove that AE ≅ CD. (In the figure, B is the common vertex on the right, A is at the top left and C at the bottom left; D lies on AB, E lies on CB, and segments AE and CD cross inside the figure.)

Ans: Given:
In the figure, △ABC has vertex B on the right, A at the top left and C at the bottom left. D is a point on AB and E is a point on CB; AE and CD are joined. AB ≅ CB and ∠A ≅ ∠C.
To Prove:
AE ≅ CD
Construction:
None.
Proof:
In △ABE ↔ △CBD — statement
∠A ≅ ∠C — reason: given
AB ≅ CB — reason: given
∠B ≅ ∠B — reason: common angle
∴ △ABE ≅ △CBD — reason: A.S.A ≅ A.S.A
Hence AE ≅ CD — reason: corresponding sides of congruent triangles
Hence proved.

Q: Q4. ABC is a triangle in which m∠A = 35° and m∠B = 100°, BD ⊥ AC. Prove that △BDC is an isosceles triangle.

Ans: Given:
In △ABC, m∠A = 35°, m∠B = 100°, and BD ⊥ AC with D on AC (produced if needed), so ∠BDC = 90°.
To Prove:
△BDC is isosceles
Construction:
None.
Proof:
m∠C = 180° − m∠A − m∠B — reason: angle sum of a triangle
m∠C = 180° − 35° − 100° = 45°
In △BDC, m∠DBC = 180° − m∠BDC − m∠C — reason: angle sum of a triangle
m∠DBC = 180° − 90° − 45° = 45°
∴ m∠DBC = m∠C = 45°
Hence BD ≅ CD — reason: sides opposite to congruent angles are congruent
∴ △BDC is an isosceles triangle.
Hence proved.

Q: Q5. ABC is an isosceles triangle. D is the mid-point of base BC. Prove that AD bisects ∠A and AD ⊥ BC.

Ans: Given:
△ABC is isosceles with AB ≅ AC, and D is the midpoint of the base BC, so BD ≅ DC.
To Prove:
AD bisects ∠A and AD ⊥ BC
Construction:
None.
Proof:
In △ABD ↔ △ACD — statement
AB ≅ AC — reason: given (isosceles triangle)
BD ≅ DC — reason: D is the midpoint of BC (given)
AD ≅ AD — reason: common side
∴ △ABD ≅ △ACD — reason: S.S.S ≅ S.S.S
Hence ∠BAD ≅ ∠DAC — reason: corresponding angles of congruent triangles, so AD bisects ∠A
Also ∠ADB ≅ ∠ADC — reason: corresponding angles of congruent triangles
But ∠ADB + ∠ADC = 180° — reason: linear pair on BC
∴ ∠ADB = ∠ADC = 90°, so AD ⊥ BC
Hence proved.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a sufficient condition for the congruency of two triangles?
mcqs.why: Three equal angles only fix the shape, not the size: a small and a large triangle can have the same three angles without being congruent. So A.A.A is not sufficient, while A.S.A, H.S and S.A.A are sufficient conditions.

mcqs.q: The diagonal of which figure does NOT divide it into two congruent triangles?
mcqs.why: A diagonal of a rectangle, square or parallelogram creates two triangles matched by S.S.S (opposite sides equal, diagonal common). A general trapezium has no such equal-side pairing, so its diagonal does not give two congruent triangles.

mcqs.q: If triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF in that correspondence, which of the following is NOT correct?
options: Angle B is congruent to angle E
Angle CBA is congruent to angle FED
Angle ABC is congruent to angle EFD
mcqs.why: In the correspondence A-D, B-E, C-F, angle ABC has its vertex at B, so it must correspond to the angle with vertex E, namely angle DEF. Angle EFD has vertex F, so angle ABC congruent to angle EFD does not follow and is not correct.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, if angle A is congruent to angle B, then the bisector of which angle divides triangle ABC into two congruent triangles?
mcqs.why: Angle A congruent to angle B means the opposite sides are equal, so the triangle is isosceles with the apex at C. The bisector of the vertex angle C meets the base at its midpoint and, by S.A.S, divides the triangle into two congruent triangles.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a legitimate reason for declaring two triangles to be congruent?
mcqs.why: SAS (two sides and the included angle) is a valid congruence postulate. SSA does not fix a unique triangle, and AAA fixes only shape, not size, so neither is legitimate.

mcqs.q: In triangle PQR the bisectors of angles Q and R meet at O. Why is O equidistant from the sides of the triangle?
options: Because every point on an angle bisector is equidistant from the arms of that angle
Because O is the midpoint of QR
mcqs.why: Drop perpendiculars OL, OM, ON from O to the three sides. O lies on the bisector of angle Q, so OL = OM; O also lies on the bisector of angle R, so OM = ON. Hence OL = OM = ON, and O is equidistant from all three sides.

mcqs.q: In the figure for triangle ABC, AB is congruent to CB, angle A is congruent to angle C, D lies on AB and E lies on CB. AE is proved congruent to CD using triangles ABE and CBD. Which postulate and which common part are used?
mcqs.why: In triangles ABE and CBD: angle A is congruent to angle C (given), AB is congruent to CB (given), and angle B is common to both triangles. Angle-side-angle with the common angle B gives A.S.A congruence, so corresponding sides AE and CD are congruent.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, angle A = 35 degrees, angle B = 100 degrees, and BD is perpendicular to AC. What is angle C, and why is triangle BDC isosceles?
options: Angle C = 55 degrees; because BD = AC
Angle C = 45 degrees; because angle DBC = angle C = 45 degrees, so BD = CD
Angle C = 35 degrees; because all angles are equal
Angle C = 65 degrees; because angle DBC = 90 degrees
mcqs.why: Angle sum: angle C = 180 - 35 - 100 = 45 degrees. In triangle BDC, angle DBC = 180 - 90 - 45 = 45 degrees. Since angle DBC = angle C, the opposite sides BD and CD are congruent, so triangle BDC is isosceles.

mcqs.q: ABC is isosceles with D the midpoint of base BC. By which postulate are triangles ABD and ACD congruent in the proof that AD bisects angle A and AD is perpendicular to BC?
mcqs.why: AB is congruent to AC (isosceles, given), BD is congruent to DC (D is the midpoint of BC), and AD is a common side. Three pairs of congruent sides give S.S.S congruence; the angle bisection and the 90-degree angles then follow from corresponding parts.

mcqs.q: Which fact about corresponding parts is used after proving two triangles congruent?
options: Corresponding sides and angles of congruent triangles are congruent
All sides of any triangle are equal
mcqs.why: Once triangles are proved congruent by a postulate such as S.S.S, S.A.S, A.S.A or H.L, every remaining matching part is also congruent. This corresponding-parts fact is what yields conclusions like BD = CE and AE = CD in the proofs.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.1
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In a parallelogram, opposite angles are congruent and consecutive angles are supplementary (they add up to 180 degrees).
  • In a parallelogram, opposite sides are congruent.
  • An exterior angle of a parallelogram and its adjacent interior angle form a linear pair, so they add up to 180 degrees.
  • By the Triangle Midsegment Theorem, the segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is half the length of the third side and parallel to it.
  • The diagonals of a rhombus bisect its angles.
  • The diagonals of a rectangle are congruent.
  • The centroid of a triangle divides each median in the ratio 2 : 1, the longer part being towards the vertex.
  • Joining the midpoints of the three sides of a triangle forms four triangles that are congruent to one another.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. Measure of one of the angles of parallelogram is 70°. Find the measure of the remaining angles.

Ans: In a parallelogram, opposite angles are congruent and consecutive angles are supplementary.
Let the given angle be 70°.
Its opposite angle = 70°
Each consecutive angle = 180° − 70° = 110°
Answer: The remaining angles are 110°, 70° and 110°.

Q: Q2. Measure of one of the exterior angles of a parallelogram is 125°. Find the measure of all of its interior angles.

Ans: An exterior angle and its adjacent interior angle form a linear pair.
Adjacent interior angle = 180° − 125° = 55°
In a parallelogram, opposite angles are congruent and consecutive angles are supplementary.
The angle opposite to 55° is 55°.
Each of the other two angles = 180° − 55° = 125°
Answer: The interior angles are 55°, 125°, 55° and 125°.

Q: Q3. RSTU is a parallelogram. Find ST. (In the figure, RU = 3n − 20 and ST = n + 12 are opposite sides.)

Ans: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are congruent.
RU = ST
3n − 20 = n + 12
3n − n = 12 + 20
2n = 32
n = 16
ST = n + 12 = 16 + 12 = 28
Answer: ST = 28

Q: Q4(i). Find the value of each variable in the parallelogram using the properties. (Figure i: a parallelogram with left side x, top side y, right side 9 and bottom side 15.)

Ans: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are congruent.
x is opposite the side 9, so x = 9
y is opposite the side 15, so y = 15
Answer: x = 9, y = 15

Q: Q4(ii). Find the value of each variable in the parallelogram using the properties. (Figure ii: a parallelogram with left side n, top side m + 1, right side 12 and bottom side 6.)

Ans: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are congruent.
n is opposite the side 12, so n = 12
m + 1 is opposite the side 6, so m + 1 = 6
m = 5
Answer: n = 12, m = 5

Q: Q4(iii). Find the value of each variable in the parallelogram using the properties. (Figure iii: a parallelogram with top right angle 120° and bottom left angle 2p°.)

Ans: In a parallelogram, opposite angles are congruent.
2p° is opposite the angle 120°.
2p = 120
p = 60
Answer: p = 60

Q: Q4(iv). Find the value of each variable in the parallelogram using the properties. (Figure iv: a parallelogram with left side 20, top right angle (d − 21)°, right side z − 8 and bottom left angle 105°.)

Ans: In a parallelogram, opposite sides and opposite angles are congruent.
(d − 21)° is opposite the angle 105°, so d − 21 = 105
d = 126
z − 8 is opposite the side 20, so z − 8 = 20
z = 28
Answer: d = 126, z = 28

Q: Q5(i). DE is a midsegment of △ABC. Find the value of x. (Figure i: D is on AB, E is on AC, DE = x and BC = 26.)

Ans: By the Triangle Midsegment Theorem, a midsegment is half the length of the third side.
DE = (1/2)BC
x = (1/2)(26)
x = 13
Answer: x = 13

Q: Q5(ii). DE is a midsegment of △ABC. Find the value of x. (Figure ii: D is on BC, E is on AC, DE = 5 and AB = x, with DE parallel to AB.)

Ans: By the Triangle Midsegment Theorem, a midsegment is half the length of the side it is parallel to.
DE = (1/2)AB
5 = (1/2)x
x = 10
Answer: x = 10

Q: Q5(iii). DE is a midsegment of △ABC. Find the value of x. (Figure iii: D is on BC, E is on AC, AB = 6 and DE = x, with DE parallel to AB.)

Ans: By the Triangle Midsegment Theorem, a midsegment is half the length of the side it is parallel to.
DE = (1/2)AB
x = (1/2)(6)
x = 3
Answer: x = 3

Q: Q6. Prove that diagonals of a rhombus bisect its angles.

Ans: Given:
ABCD is a rhombus, so AB ≅ BC ≅ CD ≅ DA. Diagonal AC joins A to C and diagonal BD joins B to D.
To Prove:
Each diagonal bisects the angles at the vertices it joins, e.g. AC bisects ∠A and ∠C
Construction:
None.
Proof:
In △ABC ↔ △ADC — statement
AB ≅ AD — reason: sides of a rhombus are congruent
CB ≅ CD — reason: sides of a rhombus are congruent
AC ≅ AC — reason: common side
∴ △ABC ≅ △ADC — reason: S.S.S ≅ S.S.S
Hence ∠BAC ≅ ∠DAC — reason: corresponding angles of congruent triangles, so AC bisects ∠A
Also ∠BCA ≅ ∠DCA — reason: corresponding angles of congruent triangles, so AC bisects ∠C
Similarly, diagonal BD bisects ∠B and ∠D.
Hence the diagonals of a rhombus bisect its angles.
Hence proved.

Q: Q7. In rhombus MNOP, m∠N = 60°. What is m∠O?

Ans: A rhombus is a parallelogram, and in a parallelogram consecutive angles are supplementary.
∠N and ∠O are consecutive angles of rhombus MNOP.
m∠N + m∠O = 180°
60° + m∠O = 180°
m∠O = 120°
Answer: m∠O = 120°

Q: Q8. Prove that diagonals of a rectangle are congruent.

Ans: Given:
ABCD is a rectangle, so all its angles are right angles and opposite sides are congruent. AC and BD are its diagonals.
To Prove:
AC ≅ BD
Construction:
None.
Proof:
In △ABC ↔ △BAD — statement
BC ≅ AD — reason: opposite sides of a rectangle are congruent
∠ABC ≅ ∠BAD — reason: each is a right angle
AB ≅ BA — reason: common side
∴ △ABC ≅ △BAD — reason: S.A.S ≅ S.A.S
Hence AC ≅ BD — reason: corresponding sides of congruent triangles
Hence the diagonals of a rectangle are congruent.
Hence proved.

Q: Q9. In a △ABC, D and E are two points on AB and AC, such that mAD = (1/4)mAB and mAE = (1/4)mAC. Prove that mDE = (1/4)mBC.

Ans: Given:
In △ABC, D is a point on AB with AD = (1/4)AB and E is a point on AC with AE = (1/4)AC. DE is joined.
To Prove:
mDE = (1/4)mBC
Construction:
Take F, the midpoint of AB, and G, the midpoint of AC, and join FG.
Proof:
FG = (1/2)BC — reason: Triangle Midsegment Theorem in △ABC
AD = (1/4)AB = (1/2)AF, so D is the midpoint of AF — statement
AE = (1/4)AC = (1/2)AG, so E is the midpoint of AG — statement
∴ DE = (1/2)FG — reason: Triangle Midsegment Theorem in △AFG
DE = (1/2) × (1/2)BC = (1/4)BC
∴ mDE = (1/4)mBC
Hence proved.

Q: Q10(i). G is the centroid of △ABC, BG = 6, AF = 12 and AE = 15. Find the length of the segment FC. (In the figure, F is the midpoint of AC on the median BF, E is the midpoint of BC on the median AE, and the medians meet at the centroid G.)

Ans: F is the midpoint of AC, so AF = FC.
AF = 12
Answer: FC = 12

Q: Q10(ii). G is the centroid of △ABC, BG = 6, AF = 12 and AE = 15. Find the length of the segment BF.

Ans: The centroid divides a median in the ratio 2 : 1, so BG = (2/3)BF.
6 = (2/3)BF
BF = 6 × 3/2 = 9
Answer: BF = 9

Q: Q10(iii). G is the centroid of △ABC, BG = 6, AF = 12 and AE = 15. Find the length of the segment AG.

Ans: The centroid divides a median in the ratio 2 : 1, so AG = (2/3)AE.
AG = (2/3)(15) = 10
Answer: AG = 10

Q: Q10(iv). G is the centroid of △ABC, BG = 6, AF = 12 and AE = 15. Find the length of the segment GE.

Ans: The centroid divides a median in the ratio 2 : 1, so GE = (1/3)AE.
GE = (1/3)(15) = 5
Answer: GE = 5

Q: Q11. Prove that the four triangles formed by joining the mid points of the three sides of a triangle are congruent to one another.

Ans: Given:
In △ABC, D, E and F are the midpoints of BC, CA and AB respectively. DE, EF and FD are joined, forming four triangles: △AFE, △FBD, △ECD and △DEF.
To Prove:
The four triangles are congruent to one another
Construction:
None.
Proof:
DE = (1/2)AB — reason: Triangle Midsegment Theorem (D, E are midpoints of BC, CA)
∴ DE ≅ AF ≅ FB — reason: F is the midpoint of AB, so AF = FB = (1/2)AB
Similarly EF ≅ BD ≅ DC and FD ≅ AE ≅ EC — reason: Triangle Midsegment Theorem and the midpoint data
In △AFE ↔ △FBD — statement
AF ≅ FB, AE ≅ BD, FE ≅ DF — reason: proved above (each segment equals half of a side of △ABC)
∴ △AFE ≅ △FBD — reason: S.S.S ≅ S.S.S
Similarly △AFE ≅ △ECD and △AFE ≅ △DEF — reason: S.S.S ≅ S.S.S, by the same half-side equalities
Hence all four triangles are congruent to one another.
Hence proved.

Q: Q12. In the given △ABC, D and E are the mid-points of AB and AC, and mCF = (1/2)mBC. Prove that mCG = (1/3)mAG. (In the figure, BC is produced beyond C to F with CF = (1/2)BC, and DF is joined, meeting AC at G.)

Ans: Given:
In △ABC, D is the midpoint of AB and E is the midpoint of AC. On BC produced beyond C, point F is taken with CF = (1/2)BC. Segment DF meets AC at G.
To Prove:
mCG = (1/3)mAG
Construction:
Through D, draw DH parallel to AC, meeting BC at H.
Proof:
D is the midpoint of AB and DH ∥ AC — statement (construction)
∴ H is the midpoint of BC — reason: converse of the Triangle Midsegment Theorem in △ABC
∴ DH = (1/2)AC — reason: Triangle Midsegment Theorem
Also HC = (1/2)BC = CF — reason: H is the midpoint of BC, and CF = (1/2)BC (given)
∴ C is the midpoint of HF — reason: HC = CF, with H, C, F collinear
In △DHF, C is the midpoint of HF and CG ∥ DH — statement (CG is part of AC, and DH ∥ AC by construction)
∴ CG = (1/2)DH — reason: converse of the Triangle Midsegment Theorem in △DHF
∴ CG = (1/2) × (1/2)AC = (1/4)AC
AG = AC − CG = (3/4)AC
∴ CG/AG = (1/4)/(3/4) = 1/3
∴ mCG = (1/3)mAG
Hence proved.

mcqs.q: One angle of a parallelogram measures 70 degrees. What is the measure of each angle consecutive to it?
mcqs.why: Consecutive angles of a parallelogram are supplementary. Working: consecutive angle = 180 degrees - 70 degrees = 110 degrees.

mcqs.q: One angle of a parallelogram measures 70 degrees. What is the measure of the angle opposite to it?
mcqs.why: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are congruent, so the angle opposite the 70 degree angle also measures 70 degrees.

mcqs.q: One exterior angle of a parallelogram measures 125 degrees. What is the measure of the adjacent interior angle?
mcqs.why: An exterior angle and its adjacent interior angle form a linear pair. Working: interior angle = 180 degrees - 125 degrees = 55 degrees.

mcqs.q: RSTU is a parallelogram with opposite sides RU = 3n - 20 and ST = n + 12. What is the value of n?
mcqs.why: Opposite sides are congruent, so RU = ST. Working: 3n - 20 = n + 12, so 2n = 32, and therefore n = 16.

mcqs.q: RSTU is a parallelogram with RU = 3n - 20, ST = n + 12 and n = 16. What is the length ST?
mcqs.why: Working: ST = n + 12. Substituting n = 16 gives ST = 16 + 12 = 28.

mcqs.q: In a parallelogram, side x is opposite a side of length 9 and side y is opposite a side of length 15. What are x and y?
mcqs.why: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are congruent. Working: x is opposite 9 so x = 9, and y is opposite 15 so y = 15.

mcqs.q: In a parallelogram, an angle of 2p degrees is opposite an angle of 120 degrees. What is p?
mcqs.why: Opposite angles are congruent. Working: 2p = 120, so p = 120 / 2 = 60.

mcqs.q: DE is a midsegment of triangle ABC with DE = x and BC = 26. What is x?
mcqs.why: By the Triangle Midsegment Theorem, DE = (1/2)BC. Working: x = (1/2) x 26 = 13.

mcqs.q: DE is a midsegment of triangle ABC, parallel to AB, with DE = 5 and AB = x. What is x?
mcqs.why: A midsegment is half the side it is parallel to. Working: DE = (1/2)AB, so 5 = (1/2)x, giving x = 10.

mcqs.q: What do the diagonals of a rhombus do to its angles?
options: They make the angles right angles
mcqs.why: The proof using SSS congruence of the two triangles formed by a diagonal shows the diagonal splits each vertex angle into two congruent parts, so the diagonals of a rhombus bisect its angles.

mcqs.q: In rhombus MNOP, m angle N = 60 degrees. What is m angle O?
mcqs.why: A rhombus is a parallelogram, so consecutive angles are supplementary. Working: m angle O = 180 degrees - 60 degrees = 120 degrees.

mcqs.q: What is true about the diagonals of a rectangle?
mcqs.why: The proof by SAS congruence of triangles ABC and BAD shows the corresponding sides AC and BD are equal, so the diagonals of a rectangle are congruent.

mcqs.q: G is the centroid of triangle ABC. The median BF is split by G with BG = 6. What is the length BF?
mcqs.why: The centroid divides a median in the ratio 2 : 1, so BG = (2/3)BF. Working: 6 = (2/3)BF, so BF = 6 x 3/2 = 9.

mcqs.q: G is the centroid of triangle ABC and the median AE = 15. What are AG and GE?
mcqs.why: The centroid divides the median in the ratio 2 : 1. Working: AG = (2/3) x 15 = 10 and GE = (1/3) x 15 = 5, and 10 + 5 = 15 as a check.

mcqs.q: The midpoints of the three sides of a triangle are joined. What is true about the four triangles formed?
options: Only two of them are congruent
They are all congruent to one another
mcqs.why: Each side of each small triangle equals half of a side of the original triangle by the Midsegment Theorem, so the four triangles are congruent to one another by SSS.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 11
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A square is the quadrilateral whose diagonals are both congruent and perpendicular.
  • The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular to each other and bisect the opposite angles of the rhombus.
  • The centroid is the point of concurrency of the medians of a triangle, and it divides each median in the ratio 2 : 1.
  • The sum of the measures of the interior angles of a quadrilateral is 360 degrees, that is 4 right angles.
  • If opposite angles of a quadrilateral are equal in measure, the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.
  • Joining the midpoints of the sides of a quadrilateral in order forms a parallelogram.
  • Joining the midpoints of the sides of an equilateral triangle forms 4 equilateral triangles.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Which quadrilateral must have diagonals that are congruent and perpendicular?

Options: (a) Rhombus (b) Square (c) Trapezoid (d) Parallelogram

Correct answer: Square

Q: Q1(ii). How many equilateral triangles can be made by joining the midpoints of the sides of an equilateral triangle.

Options: (a) 2 (b) 3 (c) 4 (d) cannot be determined

Correct answer: 4

Q: Q1(iii). Which statement must be true?

Options: (a) If a parallelogram is not a rectangle, then it is not a square. (b) If a parallelogram is not a square, then it is not a rectangle. (c) All rectangles are squares. (d) If a parallelogram is a rectangle, then it is a square.

Correct answer: If a parallelogram is not a rectangle, then it is not a square.

Q: Q1(iv). Which quadrilateral's diagonals are perpendicular to each other and bisect the figure's opposite angles?

Options: (a) Trapezoid (b) Rectangle (c) Rhombus (d) Parallelogram

Correct answer: Rhombus

Q: Q1(v). If opposite angles of a quadrilateral are equal in measure and none of them is a right angle, then the quadrilateral is a

Options: (a) Square (b) Parallelogram (c) Trapezoid (d) Rectangle

Correct answer: Parallelogram

Q: Q1(vi). Medians of a triangle are divided by the point of concurrency in the ratio

Options: (a) 2 : 1 (b) 2 : 3 (c) 1 : 3 (d) None of these

Correct answer: 2 : 1

Q: Q1(vii). Centroid is the point of concurrency of

Options: (a) medians of a triangle (b) Angle bisectors of a triangle (c) Altitudes of a triangle (d) Perpendicular bisectors of a triangle.

Correct answer: medians of a triangle

Q: Q1(viii). If sum of the measures of ∠A and ∠C of a parallelogram ABCD is 120°, then m∠B =

Options: (a) 25° (b) 50° (c) 65° (d) None of these

Correct answer: None of these

Q: Q1(ix). Diagonals of a square are ________ to each other.

Options: (a) Perpendicular (b) Not congruent (c) Congruent (d) Parallel

Correct answer: Perpendicular

Q: Q1(x). Sum of the measures of interior angles of a quadrilateral is

Options: (a) 2 right angles (b) 4 right angles (c) 3 right angles (d) None of these

Correct answer: 4 right angles

Q: Q2. Measure of one of the angles of parallelogram is 60°. Find the measure of the remaining angles.

Ans: In a parallelogram, opposite angles are congruent and consecutive angles are supplementary.
The angle opposite to 60° is 60°.
Each consecutive angle = 180° − 60° = 120°
Answer: The remaining angles are 120°, 60° and 120°.

Q: Q3. Measure of one of the exterior angles of a parallelogram is 130°. Find the measure of all of its interior angles.

Ans: An exterior angle and its adjacent interior angle form a linear pair.
Adjacent interior angle = 180° − 130° = 50°
In a parallelogram, opposite angles are congruent and consecutive angles are supplementary.
The angle opposite to 50° is 50°.
Each of the other two angles = 180° − 50° = 130°
Answer: The interior angles are 50°, 130°, 50° and 130°.

Q: Q4. Prove that the line segments joining the mid-points of the sides of a quadrilateral taken in order, form a parallelogram.

Ans: Given:
ABCD is a quadrilateral. P, Q, R and S are the midpoints of AB, BC, CD and DA respectively, joined in order.
To Prove:
PQRS is a parallelogram
Construction:
Join the diagonal AC.
Proof:
In △ABC, PQ = (1/2)AC and PQ ∥ AC — reason: Triangle Midsegment Theorem (P, Q midpoints of AB, BC)
In △ADC, SR = (1/2)AC and SR ∥ AC — reason: Triangle Midsegment Theorem (S, R midpoints of AD, DC)
∴ PQ ≅ SR and PQ ∥ SR — reason: both equal (1/2)AC and both parallel to AC
∴ PQRS has one pair of opposite sides congruent and parallel
Hence PQRS is a parallelogram.
Hence proved.

Q: Q5. In rhombus MNOP, m∠N = 70°. What is m∠O?

Ans: A rhombus is a parallelogram, and in a parallelogram consecutive angles are supplementary.
∠N and ∠O are consecutive angles of rhombus MNOP.
m∠N + m∠O = 180°
70° + m∠O = 180°
m∠O = 110°
Answer: m∠O = 110°

Q: Q6. Measure of one of the angles of parallelogram is 50°. Find the measure of the remaining angles.

Ans: In a parallelogram, opposite angles are congruent and consecutive angles are supplementary.
The angle opposite to 50° is 50°.
Each consecutive angle = 180° − 50° = 130°
Answer: The remaining angles are 130°, 50° and 130°.

Q: Note

Ans: For Q1(ix) above: the book's printed answer key gives (d) Parallel, which is incorrect — the diagonals of a square are perpendicular (and also congruent); they are never parallel. The correct option is (a) Perpendicular.

mcqs.q: Which quadrilateral must have diagonals that are congruent and perpendicular?
mcqs.why: A square has diagonals that are congruent, like a rectangle, and perpendicular, like a rhombus, so the square is the quadrilateral with both properties.

mcqs.q: How many equilateral triangles are formed by joining the midpoints of the sides of an equilateral triangle?
mcqs.why: Joining the three midpoints divides an equilateral triangle into four small triangles, and all four are equilateral and congruent to one another.

mcqs.q: Which statement must be true?
options: If a parallelogram is not a rectangle, then it is not a square.
If a parallelogram is not a square, then it is not a rectangle.
If a parallelogram is a rectangle, then it is a square.
mcqs.why: Every square is a rectangle, so a parallelogram that is not a rectangle cannot be a square. The other statements are false because a rectangle need not be a square.

mcqs.q: Which quadrilateral has diagonals that are perpendicular to each other and bisect the opposite angles?
mcqs.why: The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular bisectors of each other and, as proved in Exercise 11.1, each diagonal bisects the angles at the vertices it joins.

mcqs.q: If opposite angles of a quadrilateral are equal in measure and none of them is a right angle, then the quadrilateral is a
mcqs.why: Equal opposite angles make the quadrilateral a parallelogram. It is not a rectangle or square because none of its angles is a right angle.

mcqs.q: The medians of a triangle are divided by their point of concurrency in the ratio
mcqs.why: The centroid divides each median in the ratio 2 : 1, with the part towards the vertex twice as long as the part towards the side.

mcqs.q: The centroid is the point of concurrency of
mcqs.why: By definition, the centroid is the single point where the three medians of a triangle meet, that is, their point of concurrency.

mcqs.q: In parallelogram ABCD, m angle A + m angle C = 120 degrees. What is m angle B?
mcqs.why: Angles A and C are opposite, so each is 120 / 2 = 60 degrees. Working: angle B is consecutive to A, so m angle B = 180 degrees - 60 degrees = 120 degrees.

mcqs.q: The diagonals of a square are ______ to each other.
mcqs.why: The diagonals of a square bisect each other at right angles, so they are perpendicular to each other (they are also congruent).

mcqs.q: The sum of the measures of the interior angles of a quadrilateral is
mcqs.why: A quadrilateral splits into two triangles, and each triangle has angle sum 180 degrees. Working: 2 x 180 degrees = 360 degrees = 4 right angles.

chapters.title: Unit 12: Line Bisectors and Angle Bisectors

lessons.title: Exercise 12.1
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • If the diagonals of a quadrilateral are the right bisectors of each other, then all the sides of the quadrilateral are congruent.
  • Any point on the perpendicular bisector (right bisector) of a segment is equidistant from the endpoints of the segment.
  • The perpendicular bisector of a segment passes through the midpoint of the segment at right angles, so it makes the two parts of the segment equal.
  • Any point on the bisector of an angle is equidistant from the arms of the angle, where distance means perpendicular distance.
  • Conversely, a point inside an angle that is equidistant from its arms (by perpendicular distances) lies on the bisector of the angle.
  • In an isosceles triangle, the bisector of the vertex angle is also the perpendicular bisector of the base, so it passes through the midpoint of the base.
  • The diagonals of a square are the right bisectors of each other.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. If the diagonals of a quadrilateral are the right bisectors of each other, then prove that all the sides of the quadrilateral are congruent.

Ans: Given:
In quadrilateral ABCD, the diagonals AC and BD bisect each other at right angles at E, so AE ≅ EC, BE ≅ ED, and AC ⊥ BD.
To Prove:
AB ≅ BC ≅ CD ≅ DA
Construction:
None.
Proof:
In △AEB ↔ △CEB — statement
AE ≅ CE — reason: diagonals bisect each other (given)
∠AEB ≅ ∠CEB — reason: each is a right angle (diagonals are right bisectors)
BE ≅ BE — reason: common side
∴ △AEB ≅ △CEB — reason: S.A.S ≅ S.A.S
Hence AB ≅ CB — reason: corresponding sides of congruent triangles
Similarly △CEB ≅ △CED gives CB ≅ CD, △CED ≅ △AED gives CD ≅ DA, and △AED ≅ △AEB gives DA ≅ AB — reason: S.A.S ≅ S.A.S in each pair
∴ AB ≅ BC ≅ CD ≅ DA
Hence all the sides of the quadrilateral are congruent.
Hence proved.

Q: Q2. If PR and TS are ⊥ RS, PM = MT, Prove that △PRM ≅ △MTS.

Ans: Given:
PR ⊥ RS at R and TS ⊥ RS at S, so ∠PRM and ∠TSM are right angles. PT and RS cross at M with PM = MT (PM ≅ MT).
To Prove:
△PRM ≅ △MTS
Construction:
None.
Proof:
In △PRM ↔ △TMS — statement
∠PRM ≅ ∠TSM — reason: each is a right angle (PR ⊥ RS, TS ⊥ RS)
PM ≅ TM — reason: given
∠PMR ≅ ∠TMS — reason: vertical angles at the crossing point M
∴ △PRM ≅ △TMS (i.e. △MTS in the book's naming) — reason: A.A.S ≅ A.A.S
Hence proved.

Q: Q3. If ∠3 ≅ ∠4 and QM bisects ∠PQR, prove that M is the midpoint of PR. (In the figure, △PQR has P at the top, Q at the bottom left and R at the bottom right; M lies on PR, QM is joined, ∠3 is the angle at P, ∠4 is the angle at R, and QM splits ∠PQR into ∠1 and ∠2.)

Ans: Given:
In △PQR, M is a point on PR and QM is joined. ∠3 (at P) ≅ ∠4 (at R), and QM bisects ∠PQR, so ∠1 ≅ ∠2 where ∠1 = ∠PQM and ∠2 = ∠MQR.
To Prove:
M is the midpoint of PR, i.e. PM ≅ MR
Construction:
None.
Proof:
∠3 ≅ ∠4 — statement (given)
∴ QR ≅ PQ — reason: sides opposite to congruent angles of △PQR are congruent, so △PQR is isosceles with vertex Q
QM bisects the vertex angle ∠PQR — statement (given)
In an isosceles triangle, the bisector of the vertex angle is also the perpendicular bisector of the base — reason: proved in Unit 10 (△PQM ≅ △RQM by S.A.S)
∴ QM bisects the base PR
Hence M is the midpoint of PR.
Hence proved.

Q: Q4. Find the length of AB. (In the figure, BD is the perpendicular bisector of AC, meeting AC at D; B lies on the bisector, AB = 5x and BC = 4x + 3.)

Ans: Any point on the perpendicular bisector of a segment is equidistant from its endpoints, so BA = BC.
5x = 4x + 3
5x − 4x = 3
x = 3
AB = 5x = 5(3) = 15
Answer: AB = 15

Q: Q5(i). In the diagram, BD is the perpendicular bisector of AC. What segment lengths are equal? (In the figure, BD meets AC at D at right angles, AD = 20, DC = 7x − 15, BD = 3x and BC = 6x − 5.)

Ans: BD is the perpendicular bisector of AC, so D is the midpoint of AC and every point of BD is equidistant from A and C.
Answer: AD = DC and AB = BC

Q: Q5(ii). In the diagram, BD is the perpendicular bisector of AC. What is the value of x? (AD = 20 and DC = 7x − 15.)

Ans: D is the midpoint of AC, so AD = DC.
20 = 7x − 15
7x = 35
x = 5
Answer: x = 5

Q: Q5(iii). In the diagram, BD is the perpendicular bisector of AC. Find AB. (BC = 6x − 5 and x = 5.)

Ans: B lies on the perpendicular bisector of AC, so AB = BC.
BC = 6x − 5 = 6(5) − 5 = 25
Answer: AB = 25

Q: Q6(i). Can we conclude that EH bisects ∠FEG? (Figure i: E is the vertex, H is a point inside the angle on the left; the segments drawn from a point of EH to the arms EF and EG are not both marked perpendicular with equal lengths — the equal marks and right-angle mark needed for the converse are missing on one side.)

Ans: By the converse of the Angle Bisector Theorem, a point inside an angle lies on its bisector only if its perpendicular distances to the two arms are equal.
In figure i the perpendicular distances from the point on EH to the arms EF and EG are not shown equal (the required equal-length and right-angle marks are not both present).
Answer: No, we cannot conclude that EH bisects ∠FEG.

Q: Q6(ii). Can we conclude that EH bisects ∠FEG? (Figure ii: from H, perpendiculars are drawn to both arms EF and EG, and the two perpendicular segments are marked congruent.)

Ans: By the converse of the Angle Bisector Theorem, any point inside an angle that is equidistant from its arms lies on the bisector of the angle.
In figure ii, H is inside ∠FEG and its perpendicular distances to EF and EG are marked equal.
∴ H lies on the bisector of ∠FEG, and EH is part of that bisector.
Answer: Yes, EH bisects ∠FEG.

Q: Q6(iii). Can we conclude that EH bisects ∠FEG? (Figure iii: from H, segments to the arms EF and EG are marked congruent, but they are not drawn perpendicular to the arms.)

Ans: Distance from a point to a line means the perpendicular distance; the converse of the Angle Bisector Theorem needs the perpendicular distances to the arms to be equal.
In figure iii the equal segments from H to the arms are not perpendicular to the arms, so they are not the distances of H from the arms.
Answer: No, we cannot conclude that EH bisects ∠FEG.

Q: Q7(i). Find the value of x. (Figure i: a point lies on the bisector of an angle — the two arms are marked with equal angle marks — and its perpendicular distances to the arms are x + 11 and 3x + 1.)

Ans: Any point on the bisector of an angle is equidistant from its arms.
x + 11 = 3x + 1
11 − 1 = 3x − x
10 = 2x
x = 5
Answer: x = 5

Q: Q7(ii). Find the value of x. (Figure ii: a point inside an angle has equal perpendicular distances to the arms, marked congruent; the two parts of the angle are 7x° and (3x + 16)°.)

Ans: The point is equidistant from the arms, so by the converse of the Angle Bisector Theorem it lies on the bisector, and the two parts of the angle are equal.
7x = 3x + 16
4x = 16
x = 4
Answer: x = 4

Q: Q7(iii). Find the value of x. (Figure iii: a point inside an angle has equal perpendicular distances to the arms, marked congruent; the two parts of the angle are (5x − 2)° and (3x + 14)°.)

Ans: The point is equidistant from the arms, so by the converse of the Angle Bisector Theorem it lies on the bisector, and the two parts of the angle are equal.
5x − 2 = 3x + 14
2x = 16
x = 8
Answer: x = 8

Q: Q8. Prove that the diagonals of a square are the right bisectors of each other.

Ans: Given:
ABCD is a square, so it is a parallelogram with all sides congruent; its diagonals AC and BD meet at E.
To Prove:
AC and BD are the right bisectors of each other, i.e. they bisect each other at right angles
Construction:
None.
Proof:
AE ≅ EC and BE ≅ ED — reason: diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other
In △AEB ↔ △CEB — statement
AB ≅ CB — reason: sides of a square are congruent
BE ≅ BE — reason: common side
AE ≅ CE — reason: proved above
∴ △AEB ≅ △CEB — reason: S.S.S ≅ S.S.S
Hence ∠AEB ≅ ∠CEB — reason: corresponding angles of congruent triangles
But ∠AEB + ∠CEB = 180° — reason: linear pair on AC
∴ ∠AEB = ∠CEB = 90°, so AC ⊥ BD
Hence the diagonals of a square bisect each other at right angles, i.e. they are the right bisectors of each other.
Hence proved.

mcqs.q: If the diagonals of a quadrilateral are the right bisectors of each other, what follows about its sides?
options: Only one pair of sides is congruent
mcqs.why: SAS congruence of the four triangles formed by the diagonals shows each side equals the next one, so all the sides of the quadrilateral are congruent.

mcqs.q: PR and TS are both perpendicular to RS, and PM = MT where PT crosses RS at M. By which congruence rule is triangle PRM congruent to triangle MTS?
options: RHS only, with no other equal parts
mcqs.why: Both triangles have a right angle, PM = TM is given, and the vertical angles at M are equal. That is two angles and a non-included side, so the triangles are congruent by AAS.

mcqs.q: In isosceles triangle PQR with angle 3 (at P) congruent to angle 4 (at R), QM bisects the vertex angle PQR. What does QM do to side PR?
options: It meets PR at its midpoint
It is perpendicular to QR only
mcqs.why: Equal base angles make triangle PQR isosceles with vertex Q. The bisector of the vertex angle of an isosceles triangle is also the perpendicular bisector of the base, so M is the midpoint of PR.

mcqs.q: BD is the perpendicular bisector of AC and B lies on it, with AB = 5x and BC = 4x + 3. What is the length AB?
mcqs.why: A point on the perpendicular bisector is equidistant from the endpoints, so AB = BC. Working: 5x = 4x + 3, so x = 3, and AB = 5 x 3 = 15.

mcqs.q: BD is the perpendicular bisector of AC, meeting it at D, with AD = 20 and DC = 7x - 15. What is x?
mcqs.why: The perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint, so AD = DC. Working: 20 = 7x - 15, so 7x = 35, and x = 5.

mcqs.q: BD is the perpendicular bisector of AC. With x = 5, BC = 6x - 5. What is AB?
mcqs.why: B is on the perpendicular bisector, so AB = BC. Working: BC = 6(5) - 5 = 30 - 5 = 25, therefore AB = 25.

mcqs.q: H lies inside angle FEG and perpendiculars from H to both arms EF and EG are marked equal. Can we conclude that EH bisects angle FEG?
options: No, because H is inside the angle
No, because the arms are unequal
Yes, by the converse of the Angle Bisector Theorem
Yes, but only if the angle is acute
mcqs.why: By the converse of the Angle Bisector Theorem, a point inside an angle that is equidistant from its arms lies on the bisector, so EH bisects angle FEG.

mcqs.q: From H, segments to the arms EF and EG are marked congruent, but they are not perpendicular to the arms. Can we conclude that EH bisects angle FEG?
options: No, distance must be the perpendicular distance
Yes, if H is inside the angle
No, because the angle is not marked
mcqs.why: Distance from a point to a line means perpendicular distance. Since the equal segments are not perpendicular to the arms, they are not the distances, and the converse of the Angle Bisector Theorem does not apply.

mcqs.q: A point on the bisector of an angle has perpendicular distances x + 11 and 3x + 1 to the two arms. What is x?
mcqs.why: A point on the angle bisector is equidistant from the arms. Working: x + 11 = 3x + 1, so 10 = 2x, and x = 5.

mcqs.q: What is true about the diagonals of a square?
options: They bisect each other but not at right angles
They are the right bisectors of each other
They do not bisect each other
They are parallel to each other
mcqs.why: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, and SSS congruence then shows the angles at the intersection are both 90 degrees, so the diagonals of a square are the right bisectors of each other.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 12
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The angle bisectors, the perpendicular bisectors of the sides, and the medians of a triangle are each concurrent: each set meets at a single point.
  • The perpendicular bisectors of a triangle are concurrent.
  • In an isosceles triangle, the perpendicular bisector of the base passes through the vertex angle.
  • The point where the angle bisectors of a triangle meet is equidistant from the sides of the triangle.
  • In an equilateral triangle, the perpendicular bisectors are also the angle bisectors.
  • The diagonals of a rhombus are the right bisectors of each other.
  • If AB is congruent to AD and BC is congruent to DC, then AC is the right bisector of BD, so AC is perpendicular to BD and bisects it.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Which of the following are concurrent?

Options: (a) Angles bisectors of a triangle (b) Perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle. (c) Medians of a triangle (d) all of these

Correct answer: all of these

Q: Q1(ii). Which of the following sometimes is inside a triangle, sometimes coincides with a side of a triangle, and sometimes falls outside of a triangle?

Options: (a) the base (b) the altitude (c) the median (d) the angle bisector

Correct answer: the altitude

Q: Q1(iii). Perpendicular bisectors of a triangle are

Options: (a) Congruent (b) Concurrent (c) Parallel to each other (d) perpendicular to each other

Correct answer: Concurrent

Q: Q1(iv). In which triangle the perpendicular bisector of the base passes through its vertex angle.

Options: (a) Right angled (b) Scalene (c) Isosceles (d) Acute-angled

Correct answer: Isosceles

Q: Q1(v). In △ABC, medians AD, BE, and CF intersect at G. If CF = 24, what is the length of FG?

Options: (a) 8 (b) 12 (c) 10 (d) 16

Correct answer: 8

Q: Q1(vi). The angle bisectors of a triangle meet at a point which is equidistant from ________ of the triangle.

Options: (a) the vertices (b) the sides (c) midpoints of the sides (d) all of these

Correct answer: the sides

Q: Q1(vii). In an equilateral triangle, all the perpendicular bisectors are

Options: (a) congruent (b) concurrent (c) the angle bisectors as well (d) parallel

Correct answer: the angle bisectors as well

Q: Q1(viii). Point of intersection of the angle bisectors of a triangle is equidistant from ________ of the triangle.

Options: (a) the vertices (b) the sides (c) mid points of the sides (d) all of these

Correct answer: the sides

Q: Q2. In the given figure AB ≅ AD and BC ≅ DC. Prove that AC ⊥ BD and BE ≅ DE. (In the figure, A is at the top and C at the bottom forming a kite; B is on the left, D on the right, the diagonals AC and BD cross at E.)

Ans: Given:
In kite ABCD, A is at the top, C at the bottom, B on the left and D on the right. AB ≅ AD and BC ≅ DC. The diagonals AC and BD intersect at E.
To Prove:
AC ⊥ BD and BE ≅ DE
Construction:
None.
Proof:
A is equidistant from B and D — reason: AB ≅ AD (given)
∴ A lies on the right bisector of BD — reason: any point equidistant from the endpoints of a segment is on its right bisector
C is equidistant from B and D — reason: BC ≅ DC (given)
∴ C lies on the right bisector of BD — reason: same theorem
∴ AC is the right bisector of BD
Hence AC ⊥ BD and AC bisects BD, i.e. BE ≅ DE.
Hence proved.

Q: Q3. Prove that the diagonals of a rhombus are the right bisectors of each other.

Ans: Given:
ABCD is a rhombus, so AB ≅ BC ≅ CD ≅ DA; its diagonals AC and BD meet at E.
To Prove:
AC and BD are the right bisectors of each other
Construction:
None.
Proof:
A is equidistant from B and D, and C is equidistant from B and D — reason: sides of a rhombus are congruent (AB ≅ AD and CB ≅ CD)
∴ both A and C lie on the right bisector of BD, so AC is the right bisector of BD — reason: any point equidistant from the endpoints of a segment is on its right bisector
Similarly, B and D are equidistant from A and C, so BD is the right bisector of AC — reason: same theorem
Hence the diagonals of a rhombus are the right bisectors of each other.
Hence proved.

Q: Q4. Prove that bisectors of the base angles of an isosceles triangle intersect each other at the right bisector of the base.

Ans: Given:
△ABC is isosceles with AB ≅ AC and base BC. The bisectors of the base angles ∠B and ∠C meet each other at O.
To Prove:
O lies on the right bisector of the base BC
Construction:
Draw the right bisector of BC, meeting BC at its midpoint M.
Proof:
∠OBC = (1/2)∠B and ∠OCB = (1/2)∠C — statement (angle bisectors)
∠B ≅ ∠C — reason: base angles of an isosceles triangle
∴ ∠OBC ≅ ∠OCB — reason: halves of congruent angles are congruent
∴ OB ≅ OC — reason: sides opposite to congruent angles in △OBC are congruent
∴ O is equidistant from B and C
Hence O lies on the right bisector of BC — reason: any point equidistant from the endpoints of a segment is on its right bisector
Hence proved.

Q: Note

Ans: For Q1(vii) above: the book's printed answer key gives (d) parallel, which is incorrect — the perpendicular bisectors of an equilateral triangle meet at one point and coincide with its angle bisectors (they are also congruent); they are never parallel. The correct option is (c) the angle bisectors as well.

mcqs.q: Which of the following sets of lines in a triangle are concurrent?
options: Angle bisectors, perpendicular bisectors of the sides, and medians
mcqs.why: Each of the three sets meets at a single point in a triangle: the angle bisectors at the incentre, the perpendicular bisectors at the circumcentre, and the medians at the centroid, so all three sets are concurrent.

mcqs.q: Which of the following sometimes lies inside a triangle, sometimes coincides with a side of the triangle, and sometimes falls outside the triangle?
mcqs.why: The foot of an altitude can fall inside the triangle, on a vertex (so the altitude coincides with a side), or outside the base in an obtuse triangle, so the altitude fits the description.

mcqs.q: The perpendicular bisectors of a triangle are
mcqs.why: The three perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle all pass through one common point, the circumcentre, so they are concurrent.

mcqs.q: In which triangle does the perpendicular bisector of the base pass through its vertex angle?
mcqs.why: In an isosceles triangle the two endpoints of the base are equidistant from the vertex, so the vertex lies on the perpendicular bisector of the base, which therefore passes through the vertex angle.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, medians AD, BE and CF intersect at G. If CF = 24, what is the length of FG?
mcqs.why: G is the centroid, which divides the median in the ratio 2 : 1, so FG = (1/3)CF. Working: FG = (1/3) x 24 = 8.

mcqs.q: The angle bisectors of a triangle meet at a point which is equidistant from ______ of the triangle.
mcqs.why: Every point on an angle bisector is equidistant from the arms of the angle, so the common point of the three bisectors is equidistant from all three sides of the triangle.

mcqs.q: In an equilateral triangle, all the perpendicular bisectors are
mcqs.why: In an equilateral triangle each perpendicular bisector of a side also bisects the opposite angle, so the perpendicular bisectors are the angle bisectors as well (they are also concurrent).

mcqs.q: In kite ABCD, AB is congruent to AD and BC is congruent to DC, and the diagonals meet at E. What is true about diagonal AC?
options: AC is the right bisector of BD, so BE is congruent to DE
AC does not meet BD at right angles
mcqs.why: A is equidistant from B and D, and C is equidistant from B and D, so both lie on the right bisector of BD. Hence AC is the right bisector of BD, giving AC perpendicular to BD and BE congruent to DE.

mcqs.q: The diagonals of a rhombus are
options: The right bisectors of each other
mcqs.why: Each vertex of a rhombus is equidistant from the endpoints of the opposite diagonal because the sides are congruent, so each diagonal is the right bisector of the other.

mcqs.q: In isosceles triangle ABC with AB congruent to AC, the bisectors of the base angles B and C meet at O. Where does O lie?
options: On the right bisector of the base BC
mcqs.why: Halves of the equal base angles are equal, so angle OBC equals angle OCB and OB = OC. A point equidistant from B and C lies on the right bisector of BC, so O lies on the right bisector of the base.

chapters.title: Unit 13: Sides and Angles of a Triangle

lessons.title: Exercise 13.1
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Triangle Inequality Theorem: the sum of the lengths of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the length of the third side.
  • The third side of a triangle is less than the sum and greater than the difference of the other two sides.
  • In a triangle, the side opposite the greater angle is longer, and the longer side has the greater angle opposite to it.
  • The shortest side of a triangle is opposite its smallest angle, and the longest side is opposite its largest angle.
  • The shortest distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular distance from the point to the line.
  • The perimeter of a triangle is greater than the sum of the measures of its three altitudes.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. In the given figure, what values of x will make a triangle possible? (In the figure, two sides of the triangle are 7 and 12 and the third side is x.)

Ans: By the Triangle Inequality Theorem, the sum of the lengths of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the length of the third side.
x + 7 > 12, so x > 5
7 + 12 > x, so x < 19
(The third condition x + 12 > 7 is true for every positive x.)
Answer: 5 < x < 19

Q: Q2. Could a triangle be formed by fastening three sticks that are 6 in., 10 in., and 3 in. long?

Ans: By the Triangle Inequality Theorem, the sum of the two shorter sides must be greater than the longest side.
6 + 3 = 9
9 < 10
The sum of the two shorter sticks is less than the longest stick.
Answer: No, a triangle could not be formed.

Q: Q3. Base QR of an isosceles triangle PQR is extended to S. Prove that mPS > mPQ.

Ans: Given:
△PQR is isosceles with PQ ≅ PR and base QR. The base QR is produced beyond R to the point S, so Q, R, S are collinear.
To Prove:
mPS > mPQ
Construction:
None.
Proof:
∠PRQ is a base angle of the isosceles triangle, so it is acute — statement
∠PRS = 180° − ∠PRQ — reason: linear pair on QS
∴ ∠PRS > 90°, i.e. ∠PRS is the largest angle of △PRS — reason: the other two angles of a triangle are acute when one is obtuse
∴ PS > PR — reason: the side opposite the greater angle is longer (PS is opposite ∠PRS, PR is opposite the smaller angle ∠PSR)
But PR ≅ PQ — reason: given (isosceles triangle)
∴ mPS > mPQ
Hence proved.

Q: Q4. The length of two sides of a triangle are 11 and 23, If the third side is x, find the range of possible values for x.

Ans: By the Triangle Inequality Theorem, the third side is less than the sum and greater than the difference of the other two sides.
x < 11 + 23 = 34
x > 23 − 11 = 12
Answer: 12 < x < 34

Q: Q5. If S is any point on the side PQ of △PQR, and S is joined to R, prove that PQ + QR > PS + SR.

Ans: Given:
S is any point on side PQ of △PQR, and S is joined to R.
To Prove:
PQ + QR > PS + SR
Construction:
None.
Proof:
In △SQR, SQ + QR > SR — reason: Triangle Inequality Theorem (sum of two sides exceeds the third)
Add PS to both sides: PS + SQ + QR > PS + SR — statement
But PS + SQ = PQ — reason: S lies on PQ, so PQ is split into PS and SQ
∴ PQ + QR > PS + SR
Hence proved.

Q: Q6. If two angles of a triangle are 45° and 70° respectively, i) which is the greater of the two opposite sides? ii) which is the shortest side of the triangle? iii) which is the longest?

Ans: The third angle = 180° − 45° − 70° = 65°
The angles of the triangle are 45°, 65° and 70°.
i) The side opposite the 70° angle is greater than the side opposite the 45° angle — reason: the side opposite the greater angle is longer
ii) The shortest side is the side opposite the smallest angle, 45°
iii) The longest side is the side opposite the largest angle, 70°
Answer: i) The side opposite 70° is the greater of the two. ii) The side opposite 45° is the shortest. iii) The side opposite 70° is the longest.

Q: Q7. If in △RST, RS > ST, and m∠S = 60°, i) which is the smallest side of the triangle? ii) which is the longest?

Ans: RS is opposite ∠T and ST is opposite ∠R.
RS > ST, so m∠T > m∠R — reason: the longer side has the greater angle opposite to it
m∠R + m∠T = 180° − m∠S = 180° − 60° = 120°
Since m∠T > m∠R and their sum is 120°, m∠R < 60° < m∠T
So the angles in order are ∠R (smallest), ∠S = 60°, ∠T (largest).
i) The smallest side is opposite the smallest angle ∠R, which is ST.
ii) The longest side is opposite the largest angle ∠T, which is RS.
Answer: i) ST is the smallest side. ii) RS is the longest side.

Q: Q8. Which of the following sets of lengths could be the lengths of the sides of a triangle: (a) 2 cm, 2 cm, 2 cm (b) 3 m, 4 m, 5 m (c) 5 cm, 8 cm, 2 cm (d) 3 m, 3 m, 2 m (e) 1(1/2) m, 5 m, 3(1/2) m (f) 2(1/2) cm, 3(1/2) cm, 4(1/2) cm

Ans: By the Triangle Inequality Theorem, the sum of the two shorter lengths must be greater than the longest length.
(a) 2 + 2 = 4 > 2 — Yes
(b) 3 + 4 = 7 > 5 — Yes
(c) 5 + 2 = 7 < 8 — No
(d) 3 + 2 = 5 > 3 — Yes
(e) 1(1/2) + 3(1/2) = 5, which is not greater than 5 — No
(f) 2(1/2) + 3(1/2) = 6 > 4(1/2) — Yes
Answer: (a), (b), (d) and (f) could be the sides of a triangle; (c) and (e) could not.

Q: Q9. AB ∥ CD. If PL and QM are the shortest distances between AB and CD then prove that PL ∥ QM. (In the figure, AB is the upper line and CD the lower line; P and Q are points on AB, L and M are the feet on CD.)

Ans: Given:
Lines AB and CD are parallel. P and Q are points on AB; PL and QM are the shortest distances from P and Q to CD, with feet L and M on CD.
To Prove:
PL ∥ QM
Construction:
None.
Proof:
The shortest distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular distance — reason: from a point outside a line, the perpendicular is the shortest distance to the line
∴ PL ⊥ CD and QM ⊥ CD — statement
Two lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel to each other
∴ PL ∥ QM
Hence proved.

Q: Q10. Prove that the perimeter of a triangle is greater than the sum of the measures of its altitudes.

Ans: Given:
△ABC has sides AB, BC, CA and altitudes p, q, r drawn to BC, CA and AB respectively.
To Prove:
AB + BC + CA > p + q + r
Construction:
None.
Proof:
The altitude to BC is the perpendicular from A to BC — statement
∴ it is shorter than the slanted segments AB and AC from A to BC — reason: from a point outside a line, the perpendicular is the shortest distance
So p < AB and p < AC
Similarly q < BA and q < BC, and r < CA and r < CB — reason: same theorem at each vertex
Adding the three pairs: 2(p + q + r) < 2(AB + BC + CA)
∴ p + q + r < AB + BC + CA
Hence the perimeter of a triangle is greater than the sum of its altitudes.
Hence proved.

mcqs.q: Two sides of a triangle are 7 and 12, and the third side is x. Which values of x make a triangle possible?
mcqs.why: By the Triangle Inequality Theorem: x + 7 > 12 gives x > 5, and 7 + 12 > x gives x < 19. Combining, 5 < x < 19.

mcqs.q: Can a triangle be formed from sticks of lengths 6 in., 10 in. and 3 in.?
options: Yes, because all lengths are positive
mcqs.why: The sum of the two shorter sides must exceed the longest side. Working: 6 + 3 = 9, and 9 < 10, so the sticks cannot form a triangle.

mcqs.q: Two sides of a triangle are 11 and 23, and the third side is x. What is the range of x?
mcqs.why: The third side is greater than the difference and less than the sum of the other two. Working: 23 - 11 = 12 and 23 + 11 = 34, so 12 < x < 34.

mcqs.q: Two angles of a triangle are 45 degrees and 70 degrees. Which side is the longest side of the triangle?
options: The side opposite the third angle
mcqs.why: Working: third angle = 180 - 45 - 70 = 65 degrees. The largest angle is 70 degrees, and the longest side is opposite the largest angle, so it is the side opposite 70 degrees.

mcqs.q: In triangle RST, RS > ST and m angle S = 60 degrees. Which is the smallest side?
options: RT is longest so ST cannot be smallest
mcqs.why: RS opposite angle T exceeds ST opposite angle R, so angle T > angle R. Their sum is 120 degrees, so angle R < 60 degrees is smallest, and the smallest side opposite it is ST.

mcqs.q: Which set of lengths could NOT be the sides of a triangle?
mcqs.why: Check the two shorter lengths against the longest. Working: 5 + 2 = 7, and 7 < 8, so 5 cm, 8 cm, 2 cm fails the Triangle Inequality and cannot form a triangle.

mcqs.q: Which set of lengths could NOT be the sides of a triangle?
mcqs.why: Working: 1.5 + 3.5 = 5, which equals the longest length 5 m instead of exceeding it. Equality gives a straight line, not a triangle, so this set is impossible.

mcqs.q: What is the shortest distance from a point outside a line to that line?
options: Any slanted segment to the line
The longest segment to the line
The perpendicular segment to the line
A segment parallel to the line
mcqs.why: From a point outside a line, the perpendicular segment is shorter than every slanted segment to the line, so the perpendicular distance is the shortest distance.

mcqs.q: AB is parallel to CD. PL and QM are the shortest distances from points P and Q on AB to CD. Why is PL parallel to QM?
options: Because PL = QM in length only
Because both PL and QM are perpendicular to CD
Because P and Q are on the same line only
mcqs.why: Shortest distances are perpendicular distances, so PL is perpendicular to CD and QM is perpendicular to CD. Two lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel to each other.

mcqs.q: How does the perimeter of a triangle compare with the sum of its three altitudes?
mcqs.why: Each altitude is a perpendicular, hence shorter than the slanted sides from the same vertex. Adding the inequalities gives twice the sum of the altitudes less than twice the perimeter, so the perimeter is greater.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 13
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two remote (opposite) interior angles.
  • In a triangle, sides are ordered the same way as their opposite angles: the greater angle has the longer side opposite to it.
  • The shortest distance from a point to a line is measured along the perpendicular from the point to the line, i.e. at 90 degrees.
  • The third side of a triangle must be greater than the difference and less than the sum of the other two sides.
  • If the sum of two sides equals the third side, no triangle is formed.
  • For a point D inside triangle ABC, DA + DB + DC is greater than half the perimeter of the triangle.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). An exterior angle of a triangle measures 120°. If measure of one of its remote interior angles is 40°, the measure of the second angle is

Options: (a) 40° (b) 80° (c) 70° (d) 120°

Correct answer: 80°

Q: Q1(ii). In △ABC, m∠A = 90°, m∠B = 53°, and m∠C = 37°. Which expression correctly relates the lengths of the sides of this triangle?

Options: (a) AB < BC < CA (b) AC < BC < AB (c) AB < AC < BC (d) BC < AC < AB

Correct answer: AB < AC < BC

Q: Q1(iii). In the figure P lies outside AB. mPR will be the shortest distance if m∠PRA is

Options: (a) 180° (b) 45° (c) 100° (d) 90°

Correct answer: 90°

Q: Q1(iv). In the given figure the point K lies outside XY. Which of the following represents the shortest distance? (In the figure, K is joined to points A, B, C, D on line XY, and KB is perpendicular to XY.)

Options: (a) mKD (b) mKC (c) mKA (d) mKB

Correct answer: mKB

Q: Q1(v). Measures of two sides of a triangle are 10 and 14. Which of the following can be its third side?

Options: (a) 2 (b) 4 (c) 22 (d) 24

Correct answer: 22

Q: Q1(vi). In △ABC, m∠A = 50° and m∠B = 30°, Which of the following is correct?

Options: (a) mBC > mAB (b) mAB > mCA (c) mBC < mCA (d) mAB < mCA

Correct answer: mAB > mCA

Q: Q1(vii). Which of the following represents the sides of a triangle?

Options: (a) 3, 4, and 5 (b) 3, 4, and 7 (c) 3, 4, and 8 (d) 3, 4, and 1

Correct answer: 3, 4, and 5

Q: Q1(viii). In △KLM, m∠K = 45°, m∠L = 55°, and m∠M = 80°. Which one of the following is the longest side?

Options: (a) KL (b) LM (c) KM (d) None of these

Correct answer: KL

Q: Q2. If two sides of a triangle are 8 in. and 12 in., what are the limiting values of the third side?

Ans: By the Triangle Inequality Theorem, the third side is less than the sum and greater than the difference of the two given sides.
Upper limit: 8 + 12 = 20 in.
Lower limit: 12 − 8 = 4 in.
Answer: The third side is greater than 4 inches and less than 20 inches.

Q: Q3. Can a triangle have its sides equal to 7 in., 5 in., and 12 in.?

Ans: By the Triangle Inequality Theorem, the sum of the two shorter sides must be greater than the longest side.
7 + 5 = 12
The sum is equal to the longest side, not greater than it.
Answer: No, a triangle cannot have sides 7 in., 5 in. and 12 in.

Q: Q4. Prove that a line drawn from the vertex of an isosceles triangle to any point in the base is shorter than either of the equal sides.

Ans: Given:
△ABC is isosceles with AB ≅ AC, A the vertex and BC the base. D is any point on the base BC, and AD is drawn.
To Prove:
AD is shorter than each equal side, i.e. AD < AB and AD < AC
Construction:
None.
Proof:
Take D on BC nearer to C (the other case is similar) — statement
∠ADB is an exterior angle of △ADC at D — statement
∴ m∠ADB > m∠C — reason: an exterior angle of a triangle is greater than either remote interior angle
But ∠C ≅ ∠B — reason: base angles of an isosceles triangle
∴ m∠ADB > m∠B
In △ABD, AD is opposite ∠B and AB is opposite ∠ADB
∴ AB > AD — reason: the side opposite the greater angle is longer
Similarly, using the exterior angle at D on the other side, AC > AD
Hence the line from the vertex to any point of the base is shorter than either equal side.
Hence proved.

Q: Q5. D is a point inside a △ABC. Prove that mDA + mDB + mDC > (1/2)(mAB + mBC + mCA)

Ans: Given:
D is any point inside △ABC, joined to the vertices A, B and C.
To Prove:
DA + DB + DC > (1/2)(AB + BC + CA)
Construction:
None.
Proof:
In △DAB, DA + DB > AB — reason: Triangle Inequality Theorem
In △DBC, DB + DC > BC — reason: Triangle Inequality Theorem
In △DCA, DC + DA > CA — reason: Triangle Inequality Theorem
Adding the three inequalities: 2(DA + DB + DC) > AB + BC + CA
Dividing by 2: DA + DB + DC > (1/2)(AB + BC + CA)
∴ mDA + mDB + mDC > (1/2)(mAB + mBC + mCA)
Hence proved.

mcqs.q: An exterior angle of a triangle measures 120 degrees. One remote interior angle measures 40 degrees. What is the other remote interior angle?
mcqs.why: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles. Working: other angle = 120 degrees - 40 degrees = 80 degrees.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, m angle A = 90 degrees, m angle B = 53 degrees and m angle C = 37 degrees. Which relation between the sides is correct?
mcqs.why: Sides are opposite the angles: AB opposite 37 degrees, AC opposite 53 degrees, BC opposite 90 degrees. In increasing angle order 37 < 53 < 90, so AB < AC < BC.

mcqs.q: P lies outside line AB and R is a point on AB. The segment PR is the shortest distance from P to AB when m angle PRA is
mcqs.why: The shortest distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular distance, which requires the segment to meet the line at a right angle, so m angle PRA must be 90 degrees.

mcqs.q: Point K lies outside line XY. K is joined to points A, B, C, D on XY, and KB is perpendicular to XY. Which segment is the shortest distance from K to XY?
mcqs.why: The perpendicular segment from a point to a line is the shortest of all segments from the point to the line. Since KB is perpendicular to XY, mKB is the shortest distance.

mcqs.q: Two sides of a triangle measure 10 and 14. Which of the following can be its third side?
mcqs.why: The third side must be greater than 14 - 10 = 4 and less than 14 + 10 = 24. Working: only 22 satisfies 4 < third side < 24; 4 and 24 are the excluded boundary values.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, m angle A = 50 degrees and m angle B = 30 degrees. Which relation is correct?
mcqs.why: Working: angle C = 180 - 50 - 30 = 100 degrees, the largest angle, so its opposite side AB is the longest. Hence mAB > mCA is correct.

mcqs.q: Which of the following can be the sides of a triangle?
mcqs.why: Working: 3 + 4 = 7 > 5, so 3, 4 and 5 works. The others fail: 3 + 4 = 7 is not greater than 7 or 8, and 3 + 1 = 4 is not greater than 4.

mcqs.q: In triangle KLM, m angle K = 45 degrees, m angle L = 55 degrees and m angle M = 80 degrees. Which side is the longest?
mcqs.why: The longest side is opposite the largest angle. The largest angle is M = 80 degrees, and the side opposite angle M is KL, so KL is the longest side.

mcqs.q: Two sides of a triangle are 8 in. and 12 in. What are the limiting values of the third side?
options: Greater than 4 in. and less than 20 in.
mcqs.why: Working: upper limit = 8 + 12 = 20 in. and lower limit = 12 - 8 = 4 in., so the third side is greater than 4 inches and less than 20 inches.

mcqs.q: Can a triangle have sides 7 in., 5 in. and 12 in.?
options: No, because the sum of the two shorter sides must be greater than, not equal to, the longest side
Yes, because all sides are positive
mcqs.why: Working: 7 + 5 = 12, which equals the longest side. The Triangle Inequality requires the sum to be strictly greater, so no triangle can have these sides.

lessons.title: Exercise 14.1
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees, so angles in a given ratio are found by dividing 180 degrees in that ratio.
  • Theorem 14.1: a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally.
  • Theorem 14.3: the internal bisector of an angle of a triangle divides the opposite side in the ratio of the sides containing the angle.
  • Theorem 14.4: corresponding sides of similar triangles are proportional.
  • Triangles are similar by AAA when their corresponding angles are congruent, for example by vertical angles and alternate interior angles for parallel lines.
  • Triangles are similar by SAS similarity when an angle of one equals an angle of the other and the including sides are proportional.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. The three angles of a triangle are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 6. What is the measure of the smallest angle?

Ans: The angles of a triangle sum to 180°.
Let the angles be x, 2x and 6x.
x + 2x + 6x = 180°
9x = 180°
x = 20°
Answer: The smallest angle is 20°.

Q: Q2. The measures of the three angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. Find the measure of the largest angle of the triangle.

Ans: The angles of a triangle sum to 180°.
Let the angles be 2x, 3x and 4x.
2x + 3x + 4x = 180°
9x = 180°
x = 20°
Largest angle = 4x = 4 × 20° = 80°
Answer: The largest angle is 80°.

Q: Q3. In the given figure, show that △QRS and △TUS are similar. (QR ∥ TU) (In the figure, lines QT and RU cross at S; Q and R are at the top with QR horizontal, T and U at the bottom with TU horizontal.)

Ans: Given:
In the figure, QT and RU intersect at S. QR is the top segment joining Q (left) to R (right), TU is the bottom segment joining T (left) to U (right), and QR ∥ TU.
To Prove:
△QRS ∼ △TUS
Construction:
None.
Proof:
∠QSR ≅ ∠TSU — reason: vertical angles at S
∠SQR ≅ ∠STU — reason: alternate interior angles (QR ∥ TU, transversal QT)
∠SRQ ≅ ∠SUT — reason: alternate interior angles (QR ∥ TU, transversal RU)
∴ △QRS ∼ △TUS — reason: A.A.A similarity (corresponding angles are congruent)
Hence proved.

Q: Q4. In the given figure show that △MNO ∼ △PQR. (In the figures, △MNO has ∠N = 40° with sides MN and NO marked with single tick marks; △PQR has ∠Q = 40° with sides PQ and QR marked with double tick marks.)

Ans: Given:
In △MNO, m∠N = 40°, and the sides about ∠N, namely MN and NO, carry the same single tick mark. In △PQR, m∠Q = 40°, and the sides about ∠Q, namely PQ and QR, carry the same double tick mark, so MN/NO and PQ/QR are the same ratio (each pair of marked sides is in the ratio 1 : 1 within its triangle, and the tick patterns show the two ratios MN : NO and PQ : QR are equal).
To Prove:
△MNO ∼ △PQR
Construction:
None.
Proof:
∠N ≅ ∠Q — reason: both measure 40° (given)
MN/PQ = NO/QR — reason: the marked (tick) sides about the equal angles are proportional, as shown in the figures
∴ △MNO ∼ △PQR — reason: S.A.S similarity (an angle of one triangle equals an angle of the other and the including sides are proportional)
Hence proved.

Q: Q5. In △ABC, DE is parallel to BC. If mAD = 1.5 cm, mBD = 3 cm, mAE = 1.3 cm, then find mCE.

Ans: A line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally (Theorem 14.1).
AD/DB = AE/EC
1.5/3 = 1.3/EC
EC = (3 × 1.3)/1.5 = 3.9/1.5 = 2.6
Answer: CE = 2.6 cm

Q: Q6. In the given figure, find the value of x. (In the figure, △ABC has B at the top, C at the right and A at the bottom left; BD is the bisector of ∠B meeting AC at D, with AB = 12, BC = 15, CD = 13 and AD = x.)

Ans: The internal bisector of an angle of a triangle divides the opposite side in the ratio of the sides containing the angle (Theorem 14.3).
AD/DC = AB/BC
x/13 = 12/15
x = (12 × 13)/15 = 156/15 = 10.4
Answer: x = 10.4

Q: Q7. In △ABC, AD is the bisector of ∠A. If mAB = 9 cm, mAC = 10 cm and mBC = 12 cm, find the measures of DC and BD.

Ans: The internal bisector of an angle of a triangle divides the opposite side in the ratio of the sides containing the angle (Theorem 14.3).
BD/DC = AB/AC = 9/10
Also BD + DC = BC = 12 cm
BD = 12 × 9/(9 + 10) = 108/19 cm ≈ 5.68 cm
DC = 12 × 10/(9 + 10) = 120/19 cm ≈ 6.32 cm
Answer: BD = 108/19 cm and DC = 120/19 cm

Q: Q8. PS is the bisector of ∠P in △PQR. If mQS = 3 cm, mSR = 7 cm and mPQ + mPR = 20 cm, find the measure of PQ and PR.

Ans: The internal bisector of an angle of a triangle divides the opposite side in the ratio of the sides containing the angle (Theorem 14.3).
PQ/PR = QS/SR = 3/7
Also PQ + PR = 20 cm
PQ = 20 × 3/(3 + 7) = 60/10 = 6 cm
PR = 20 × 7/(3 + 7) = 140/10 = 14 cm
Answer: PQ = 6 cm and PR = 14 cm

Q: Q9. ABC is a triangle in which mBC = mCA = 2mAB. Internal bisector of ∠A meets BC at D and DE is drawn parallel to CA meeting AB at E. Find mDE : mAB.

Ans: Let AB = 1 unit; then CA = 2 units and BC = 2 units.
The bisector of ∠A divides BC in the ratio of AB : AC (Theorem 14.3).
BD/DC = AB/AC = 1/2
BD = (1/3)BC = 2/3 units
In △BCA, DE ∥ CA, so DE/CA = BD/BC (Theorem 14.1, proportional segments).
DE/2 = (2/3)/2 = 1/3
DE = 2/3 units
DE : AB = 2/3 : 1 = 2 : 3
Answer: mDE : mAB = 2 : 3

Q: Q10. Measures of the sides of a triangle are 6.5 cm, 7.8 cm and 9.1 cm. Find the lengths of the segments into which the smallest side is divided by the internal bisector of the opposite angle.

Ans: The internal bisector of an angle divides the opposite side in the ratio of the adjacent sides (Theorem 14.3).
The smallest side is 6.5 cm; the sides adjacent to the opposite angle are 7.8 cm and 9.1 cm.
The segments are in the ratio 7.8 : 9.1.
First segment = 6.5 × 7.8/(7.8 + 9.1) = 50.7/16.9 = 3.0 cm
Second segment = 6.5 × 9.1/(7.8 + 9.1) = 59.15/16.9 = 3.5 cm
Answer: The segments are 3 cm and 3.5 cm.

Q: Q11. The given triangles are similar, find x. (In the figures, the smaller triangle has sides 16, x and 28; the larger similar triangle has corresponding sides 22, 33 and 38.5.)

Ans: Corresponding sides of similar triangles are proportional (Theorem 14.4).
The side 28 corresponds to 38.5, and x corresponds to 33.
x/33 = 28/38.5
x = (28 × 33)/38.5 = 924/38.5 = 24
(Check: 16/22 = 28/38.5 = 8/11, the same ratio.)
Answer: x = 24

Q: Q12. If △ABC ∼ △DEF and mAC = 12 cm, mAB = 4 cm, mBC = 10 cm and mDF = 9 cm, then find the measures of DE and EF.

Ans: Corresponding sides of similar triangles are proportional (Theorem 14.4).
AC corresponds to DF, AB corresponds to DE, and BC corresponds to EF.
AB/DE = AC/DF
4/DE = 12/9
DE = (4 × 9)/12 = 3 cm
BC/EF = AC/DF
10/EF = 12/9
EF = (10 × 9)/12 = 7.5 cm
Answer: DE = 3 cm and EF = 7.5 cm

Q: Q13. Diagonals of a trapezoid ABCD intersect each other at O. If △AOB ∼ △COD, then prove that AB ∥ CD.

Ans: Given:
ABCD is a trapezoid whose diagonals AC and BD intersect at O, and △AOB ∼ △COD.
To Prove:
AB ∥ CD
Construction:
None.
Proof:
△AOB ∼ △COD — statement (given)
∴ ∠OAB ≅ ∠OCD — reason: corresponding angles of similar triangles
∠OAB and ∠OCD are alternate interior angles for lines AB and CD with transversal AC
∴ AB ∥ CD — reason: alternate interior angles are congruent
Hence proved.

Q: Q14. In the accompanying figure, the line segment, KL, is drawn parallel to ST, intersecting RS at K and RT at L in RST. If RK = 5, KS = 10, and RT = 18, then find RL. (In the figure, R is the top vertex, S the bottom left and T the bottom right; RL = x and LT = 18 − x.)

Ans: A line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally (Theorem 14.1).
RK/KS = RL/LT
5/10 = x/(18 − x)
18 − x = 2x
18 = 3x
x = 6
Answer: RL = 6

mcqs.q: The three angles of a triangle are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 6. What is the smallest angle?
mcqs.why: Let the angles be x, 2x, 6x. Working: x + 2x + 6x = 180, so 9x = 180 and x = 20. The smallest angle is x = 20 degrees.

mcqs.q: The three angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. What is the largest angle?
mcqs.why: Let the angles be 2x, 3x, 4x. Working: 9x = 180, so x = 20. The largest angle = 4x = 4 x 20 = 80 degrees.

mcqs.q: Lines QT and RU cross at S, with QR parallel to TU. Why is triangle QRS similar to triangle TUS?
options: By SSS, because all sides are equal
By AAA, using vertical angles and alternate interior angles
mcqs.why: Angle QSR equals angle TSU (vertical angles), and the other two pairs are alternate interior angles because QR is parallel to TU. All three angles match, so the triangles are similar by AAA.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, DE is parallel to BC, with AD = 1.5 cm, BD = 3 cm and AE = 1.3 cm. What is CE?
mcqs.why: By Theorem 14.1, AD/DB = AE/EC. Working: 1.5/3 = 1.3/EC, so EC = (3 x 1.3)/1.5 = 3.9/1.5 = 2.6 cm.

mcqs.q: BD bisects angle B of triangle ABC, meeting AC at D, with AB = 12, BC = 15, CD = 13 and AD = x. What is x?
mcqs.why: By Theorem 14.3, AD/DC = AB/BC. Working: x/13 = 12/15, so x = (12 x 13)/15 = 156/15 = 10.4.

mcqs.q: AD bisects angle A in triangle ABC, with AB = 9 cm, AC = 10 cm and BC = 12 cm. What is BD?
mcqs.why: By Theorem 14.3, BD/DC = AB/AC = 9/10 and BD + DC = 12. Working: BD = 12 x 9/(9 + 10) = 108/19 cm, about 5.68 cm.

mcqs.q: PS bisects angle P in triangle PQR, with QS = 3 cm, SR = 7 cm and PQ + PR = 20 cm. What are PQ and PR?
mcqs.why: By Theorem 14.3, PQ/PR = QS/SR = 3/7. Working: PQ = 20 x 3/10 = 6 cm and PR = 20 x 7/10 = 14 cm, which add to 20 cm.

mcqs.q: The sides of a triangle are 6.5 cm, 7.8 cm and 9.1 cm. The internal bisector of the angle opposite the smallest side divides that side into segments of
mcqs.why: By Theorem 14.3 the segments are in the ratio 7.8 : 9.1. Working: first = 6.5 x 7.8/16.9 = 3.0 cm and second = 6.5 x 9.1/16.9 = 3.5 cm, totalling 6.5 cm.

mcqs.q: Two similar triangles have corresponding sides 28 and 38.5, and the side corresponding to 33 in the larger triangle is x in the smaller. What is x?
mcqs.why: Corresponding sides are proportional. Working: x/33 = 28/38.5, so x = (28 x 33)/38.5 = 924/38.5 = 24.

mcqs.q: Triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF, with AC = 12 cm, AB = 4 cm, BC = 10 cm and DF = 9 cm (AC corresponds to DF). What are DE and EF?
mcqs.why: Working: AB/DE = AC/DF gives 4/DE = 12/9, so DE = (4 x 9)/12 = 3 cm. BC/EF = AC/DF gives 10/EF = 12/9, so EF = (10 x 9)/12 = 7.5 cm.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 14
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Theorem 14.1: a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally, and this also gives ratios such as CD/CA = CE/CB.
  • SSA is not a valid test for proving triangles similar; the valid tests include AA, SSS and SAS similarity.
  • A line through the midpoint of one side of a triangle parallel to a second side bisects the third side.
  • The segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is half the third side, so the third side is twice the midsegment.
  • When two lines cross and the segments satisfy PO/OQ = RO/OS with the vertical angle between them, the triangles formed are similar by SAS similarity.
  • If AB is parallel to CD and transversals AD and BC intersect at O, then triangle AOB is similar to triangle DOC.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). In the given figure compute x? (In the figure, a line parallel to the base cuts △ABC, dividing side CA into parts 6 and x and side CB into parts 4 and 2.)

Options: (a) 7 (b) 9 (c) 2 (d) 3

Correct answer: 3

Q: Q1(ii). Which of the following is not valid for proving triangles similarity?

Options: (a) SSS (b) AA (c) SSA (d) SAS

Correct answer: SSA

Q: Q1(iii). In a mathematics class with 32 students, the ratio of girls to boys is 5 to 3. How many more girls are there than boys?

Options: (a) 2 (b) 12 (c) 8 (d) 20

Correct answer: 8

Q: Q1(iv). The measure of a line segment joining the midpoints of AB and AC of △ABC is 3.5 cm. Find mBC =

Options: (a) 4.5 cm (b) 5.5 cm (c) 6 cm (d) 7 cm

Correct answer: 7 cm

Q: Q1(v). In the figure AB ∥ CD. If AD and BC intersects at O. Then △AOB and △DOC are

Options: (a) Congruent (b) similar (c) Not similar (d) none of these

Correct answer: similar

Q: Q2. Prove that a line passing through the midpoint of one side of a triangle and parallel to a second side bisects the third side of the triangle.

Ans: Given:
In △ABC, D is the midpoint of AB and the line through D parallel to BC meets AC at E.
To Prove:
