E is the midpoint of AC, i.e. AE = EC
Construction:
None.
Proof:
DE ∥ BC — statement (given)
∴ AD/DB = AE/EC — reason: a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally (Theorem 14.1)
But AD = DB — reason: D is the midpoint of AB (given)
∴ AD/DB = 1, so AE/EC = 1
∴ AE = EC
Hence the line bisects the third side AC.
Hence proved.

Q: Q3. In the figure AB ∥ DE. If mBE = 4.1 cm, mEC = 12.3 cm and mDC = 16.5 cm, find the measure of AC. (In the figure, △CAB has C at the right, A at the top left and B at the bottom left; D lies on CA and E lies on CB, with DE parallel to AB.)

Ans: A line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally (Theorem 14.1).
In △CAB, DE ∥ AB, so CD/CA = CE/CB.
CB = CE + EB = 12.3 + 4.1 = 16.4 cm
16.5/AC = 12.3/16.4
12.3/16.4 = 3/4
AC = 16.5 × 16.4/12.3 = 16.5 × 4/3 = 22 cm
Answer: AC = 22 cm

Q: Q4. Let PQ and RS intersect at O and mPO/mOQ = mRO/mOS. Prove that △OPR ∼ △OQS.

Ans: Given:
Segments PQ and RS intersect at O, and PO/OQ = RO/OS.
To Prove:
△OPR ∼ △OQS
Construction:
None.
Proof:
PO/OQ = RO/OS — statement (given)
∠POR ≅ ∠QOS — reason: vertical angles at O
∴ △OPR ∼ △OQS — reason: S.A.S similarity (an angle of one triangle equals an angle of the other and the including sides are proportional)
Hence proved.

mcqs.q: A line parallel to the base of triangle ABC cuts side CA into parts 6 and x and side CB into corresponding parts 4 and 2. What is x?
mcqs.why: By Theorem 14.1 the parts are proportional. Working: 6/x = 4/2, so 4x = 12 and x = 3.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT valid for proving triangles similar?
mcqs.why: AA, SSS and SAS (with proportional including sides) are valid similarity tests. SSA gives no fixed shape, so SSA is not valid for proving similarity.

mcqs.q: A class of 32 students has girls to boys in the ratio 5 to 3. How many more girls are there than boys?
mcqs.why: Working: total parts = 5 + 3 = 8, so each part = 32/8 = 4 students. Girls = 5 x 4 = 20, boys = 3 x 4 = 12, difference = 20 - 12 = 8.

mcqs.q: The segment joining the midpoints of AB and AC of triangle ABC measures 3.5 cm. What is BC?
mcqs.why: The midsegment is half the third side. Working: midsegment = (1/2)BC, so BC = 2 x 3.5 cm = 7 cm.

mcqs.q: AB is parallel to CD, and AD and BC intersect at O. What is the relation between triangle AOB and triangle DOC?
mcqs.why: Vertical angles at O are equal and alternate interior angles are equal because AB is parallel to CD, so the triangles have matching angles and are similar by AA.

mcqs.q: A line passes through the midpoint of one side of a triangle and is parallel to a second side. What does it do to the third side?
options: It is parallel to the third side
It does not meet the third side
mcqs.why: By Theorem 14.1, AD/DB = AE/EC. Since D is the midpoint, AD = DB so the ratio is 1, giving AE = EC, which means the line bisects the third side.

mcqs.q: In triangle CAB, D is on CA and E is on CB with DE parallel to AB. If BE = 4.1 cm, EC = 12.3 cm and DC = 16.5 cm, what is AC?
mcqs.why: By Theorem 14.1, CD/CA = CE/CB. Working: CB = 12.3 + 4.1 = 16.4, so 16.5/AC = 12.3/16.4 = 3/4, giving AC = 16.5 x 4/3 = 22 cm.

mcqs.q: Segments PQ and RS intersect at O with PO/OQ = RO/OS. Why is triangle OPR similar to triangle OQS?
options: By SSS, because all sides are equal
By AA, because all angles are right angles
By SAS similarity, using the proportional sides about the equal vertical angle
mcqs.why: Angle POR equals angle QOS because they are vertical angles, and the sides about this angle are proportional since PO/OQ = RO/OS. Hence the triangles are similar by SAS similarity.

mcqs.q: D is the midpoint of AB in triangle ABC, and the line through D parallel to BC meets AC at E. What is AE/EC?
mcqs.why: By Theorem 14.1, AD/DB = AE/EC. Working: D is the midpoint so AD = DB and AD/DB = 1, therefore AE/EC = 1, meaning AE = EC.

mcqs.q: In triangle CAB with DE parallel to AB, D on CA and E on CB, which proportion is correct?
options: CD/CE = CA/CB only when DE = AB
mcqs.why: A line parallel to one side divides the other two sides proportionally, measured from the common vertex C. Hence CD/CA = CE/CB is the correct proportion.

lessons.title: Exercise 15.1
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Pythagoras' theorem: in a right-angled triangle, (hypotenuse)² = (perpendicular)² + (base)², i.e. c² = a² + b².
  • To find the hypotenuse, add the squares of the two sides containing the right angle and take the square root, e.g. 12² + 5² = 169, so the hypotenuse is 13 cm.
  • The diagonal of a rectangle is the hypotenuse of the right triangle formed by two adjacent sides, so d² = l² + w².
  • A ladder against a wall forms a right triangle with the ladder as hypotenuse; if a leg is unknown, subtract: (leg)² = (hypotenuse)² − (other leg)².
  • Converse of Pythagoras' theorem: a triangle is right-angled if the square of its longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides.
  • Triples such as 9, 12, 15 and 36, 48, 60 satisfy the converse (9² + 12² = 15²) and are right-angled, while 9, 10, 15 and 10, 12, 20 do not.
  • The distance between opposite corners of a rectangle is its diagonal, e.g. for 50 m by 30 m, d = √(50² + 30²) = 10√34 m ≈ 58.31 m.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. Find the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle when the sides containing the right angle are: i) 12 cm and 5 cm ii) 6 cm and 2.5 cm iii) 15 cm and 8 cm

Ans: By Pythagoras' theorem, (hypotenuse)² = (perpendicular)² + (base)².
i) h² = 12² + 5² = 144 + 25 = 169
h = √169 = 13 cm
ii) h² = 6² + 2.5² = 36 + 6.25 = 42.25
h = √42.25 = 6.5 cm
iii) h² = 15² + 8² = 225 + 64 = 289
h = √289 = 17 cm
Answer: i) 13 cm ii) 6.5 cm iii) 17 cm

Q: Q2. Find the diagonal of a rectangular field whose sides are: i) 7.2 m and 3 m ii) 15.6 m and 6.5 m iii) 6.72 m and 5.04 m

Ans: The diagonal of a rectangle is the hypotenuse of the right triangle formed by two adjacent sides, so by Pythagoras' theorem d² = l² + w².
i) d² = 7.2² + 3² = 51.84 + 9 = 60.84
d = √60.84 = 7.8 m
ii) d² = 15.6² + 6.5² = 243.36 + 42.25 = 285.61
d = √285.61 = 16.9 m
iii) d² = 6.72² + 5.04² = 45.1584 + 25.4016 = 70.56
d = √70.56 = 8.4 m
Answer: i) 7.8 m ii) 16.9 m iii) 8.4 m

Q: Q3. A ladder whose foot is 2.5 m from the front of a house reaches a window 6 m above the ground. Calculate the length of the ladder.

Ans: The wall, the ground and the ladder form a right triangle with the ladder as hypotenuse; by Pythagoras' theorem:
(length of ladder)² = 6² + 2.5²
= 36 + 6.25 = 42.25
length of ladder = √42.25 = 6.5 m
Answer: The ladder is 6.5 m long.

Q: Q4. A ladder 2.9 m long just reaches the top of a wall 2.1 m high. How far from the foot of the wall is the foot of the ladder.

Ans: The ladder is the hypotenuse and the wall is one side of a right triangle; by Pythagoras' theorem:
(distance)² = 2.9² − 2.1²
= 8.41 − 4.41 = 4.00
(distance) = √4 = 2 m
Answer: The foot of the ladder is 2 m from the foot of the wall.

Q: Q5. Find the length of the unknown side. (In the figure, the right triangle has vertical leg a, horizontal leg b and hypotenuse c.) i) a = 4 cm, b = 7 cm ii) a = 7 cm, c = 25 cm iii) b = 6 cm, c = 9 cm

Ans: By Pythagoras' theorem, c² = a² + b².
i) c² = 4² + 7² = 16 + 49 = 65
c = √65 cm ≈ 8.06 cm
ii) b² = c² − a² = 25² − 7² = 625 − 49 = 576
b = √576 = 24 cm
iii) a² = c² − b² = 9² − 6² = 81 − 36 = 45
a = √45 cm = 3√5 cm ≈ 6.71 cm
Answer: i) c = √65 cm ii) b = 24 cm iii) a = 3√5 cm

Q: Q6. Verify whether a triangle with the given side lengths is a right-angled triangle? i) 9, 12, and 15 ii) 9, 10, and 15 iii) 10, 12 and 20 iv) 36, 48, and 60

Ans: By the converse of Pythagoras' theorem, a triangle is right-angled if the square of its longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides.
i) 9² + 12² = 81 + 144 = 225 = 15² — Yes, it is a right-angled triangle.
ii) 9² + 10² = 81 + 100 = 181 ≠ 225 = 15² — No, it is not a right-angled triangle.
iii) 10² + 12² = 100 + 144 = 244 ≠ 400 = 20² — No, it is not a right-angled triangle.
iv) 36² + 48² = 1296 + 2304 = 3600 = 60² — Yes, it is a right-angled triangle.
Answer: i) Yes ii) No iii) No iv) Yes

Q: Q7. The sides of a rectangular swimming pool are 50 m and 30 m. What is the length between the opposite corners.

Ans: The distance between opposite corners is the diagonal of the rectangle; by Pythagoras' theorem:
d² = 50² + 30² = 2500 + 900 = 3400
d = √3400 = 10√34 m ≈ 58.31 m
Answer: The length between the opposite corners is 10√34 m (about 58.31 m).

mcqs.q: What does Pythagoras' theorem state for a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse c and legs a and b?
mcqs.why: Pythagoras' theorem states that the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides: c² = a² + b². This is the formula used in every item of Exercise 15.1.

mcqs.q: Find the hypotenuse when the sides containing the right angle are 12 cm and 5 cm.
mcqs.why: Full working: h² = 12² + 5² = 144 + 25 = 169. Taking the square root, h = √169 = 13 cm, so the hypotenuse is 13 cm.

mcqs.q: Find the hypotenuse when the sides containing the right angle are 6 cm and 2.5 cm.
mcqs.why: Full working: h² = 6² + 2.5² = 36 + 6.25 = 42.25. Taking the square root, h = √42.25 = 6.5 cm, so the hypotenuse is 6.5 cm.

mcqs.q: Find the diagonal of a rectangular field whose sides are 7.2 m and 3 m.
mcqs.why: The diagonal is the hypotenuse, so d² = l² + w². Full working: d² = 7.2² + 3² = 51.84 + 9 = 60.84, and d = √60.84 = 7.8 m.

mcqs.q: A ladder whose foot is 2.5 m from a house reaches a window 6 m above the ground. What is the length of the ladder?
mcqs.why: Wall, ground and ladder form a right triangle with the ladder as hypotenuse. Full working: (length)² = 6² + 2.5² = 36 + 6.25 = 42.25, so length = √42.25 = 6.5 m.

mcqs.q: A ladder 2.9 m long just reaches the top of a wall 2.1 m high. How far is the foot of the ladder from the foot of the wall?
mcqs.why: The ladder is the hypotenuse, so the unknown leg is found by subtraction. Full working: (distance)² = 2.9² − 2.1² = 8.41 − 4.41 = 4.00, so distance = √4 = 2 m.

mcqs.q: In a right triangle, a = 7 cm and the hypotenuse c = 25 cm. Find the other leg b.
mcqs.why: From c² = a² + b², b² = c² − a². Full working: b² = 25² − 7² = 625 − 49 = 576, so b = √576 = 24 cm.

mcqs.q: In a right triangle, b = 6 cm and the hypotenuse c = 9 cm. Find leg a.
mcqs.why: From c² = a² + b², a² = c² − b². Full working: a² = 9² − 6² = 81 − 36 = 45, so a = √45 = 3√5 cm ≈ 6.71 cm.

mcqs.q: Which set of side lengths forms a right-angled triangle?
mcqs.why: By the converse of Pythagoras' theorem, check the longest side. Full working: 9² + 12² = 81 + 144 = 225 = 15², so 9, 12, 15 is right-angled; the other sets fail this test.

mcqs.q: The sides of a rectangular swimming pool are 50 m and 30 m. What is the length between the opposite corners?
mcqs.why: The distance between opposite corners is the diagonal. Full working: d² = 50² + 30² = 2500 + 900 = 3400, so d = √3400 = 10√34 m ≈ 58.31 m.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 15
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • If the diagonal and one side of a rectangle are known, the other side is found by (side)² = (diagonal)² − (known side)²; diagonal 6.5 cm and width 2.5 cm give length 6 cm.
  • 3, 4, 5 is a right-angled triple because 3² + 4² = 25 = 5² (converse of Pythagoras' theorem).
  • The altitude of an equilateral triangle bisects the base; for side 8 cm, altitude² = 8² − 4² = 48, so the altitude is 4√3 cm.
  • The perpendicular from the vertex of an isosceles triangle bisects the base; with base 10 cm and perpendicular 12 cm, each congruent side is √(12² + 5²) = 13 cm.
  • If the diagonals of a quadrilateral are perpendicular, then (mAB)² + (mCD)² = (mAD)² + (mBC)², proved by applying Pythagoras' theorem in the four right triangles at the intersection point.
  • For sides x, x + 4 and hypotenuse 20, x² + (x + 4)² = 20² gives x = 12 (the negative root is rejected), so the sides are 12, 16 and 20.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Diagonal of a rectangle measures 6.5 cm. If its width is 2.5 cm, its length is

Options: (a) 4 cm (b) 9 cm (c) 6 cm (d) 3 cm

Correct answer: 6 cm

Q: Q1(ii). Which of the following are the sides of a right-angled triangle?

Options: (a) 2, 3, 4 (b) 3, 4, 5 (c) 4, 5, 6 (d) 5, 6, 7

Correct answer: 3, 4, 5

Q: Q2. Measure of each of the sides of an equilateral triangle is 8 cm. Find the length of the altitude.

Ans: The altitude of an equilateral triangle bisects the base, so it is the perpendicular from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side; by Pythagoras' theorem:
(altitude)² = 8² − 4²
= 64 − 16 = 48
altitude = √48 = 4√3 cm ≈ 6.93 cm
Answer: The altitude is 4√3 cm.

Q: Q3. Measure of the base of an isosceles triangle is 10 cm. If the perpendicular drawn from the vertex to the base is 12 cm long, find the measures of the congruent sides of the triangle.

Ans: The perpendicular from the vertex of an isosceles triangle bisects the base, so each half of the base is 5 cm; by Pythagoras' theorem:
(congruent side)² = 12² + 5²
= 144 + 25 = 169
congruent side = √169 = 13 cm
Answer: Each congruent side measures 13 cm.

Q: Q4. Diagonals of a quadrilateral ABCD are perpendicular to each other. Prove that (mAB)² + (mCD)² = (mAD)² + (mBC)².

Ans: Given:
In quadrilateral ABCD, the diagonals AC and BD are perpendicular to each other and intersect at E.
To Prove:
AB² + CD² = AD² + BC²
Construction:
None.
Proof:
In right △AEB, AB² = AE² + BE² — reason: Pythagoras' theorem
In right △CED, CD² = CE² + DE² — reason: Pythagoras' theorem
Adding: AB² + CD² = AE² + BE² + CE² + DE² — statement
In right △AED, AD² = AE² + DE² — reason: Pythagoras' theorem
In right △BEC, BC² = BE² + CE² — reason: Pythagoras' theorem
Adding: AD² + BC² = AE² + DE² + BE² + CE² — statement
The two sums are the same
∴ AB² + CD² = AD² + BC², i.e. (mAB)² + (mCD)² = (mAD)² + (mBC)²
Hence proved.

Q: Q5. The sides of a triangle have lengths x, x + 4, and 20. If the length of the longest side is 20, what values of x make the right triangle?

Ans: For a right triangle with hypotenuse 20, by Pythagoras' theorem:
x² + (x + 4)² = 20²
x² + x² + 8x + 16 = 400
2x² + 8x − 384 = 0
x² + 4x − 192 = 0
(x + 16)(x − 12) = 0
x = 12 or x = −16
A length cannot be negative, so x = −16 is rejected.
Answer: x = 12 (the sides are 12, 16 and 20).

mcqs.q: The diagonal of a rectangle measures 6.5 cm. If its width is 2.5 cm, what is its length?
mcqs.why: The diagonal is the hypotenuse, so length² = diagonal² − width². Full working: length² = 6.5² − 2.5² = 42.25 − 6.25 = 36, so length = √36 = 6 cm.

mcqs.q: Which of the following are the sides of a right-angled triangle?
mcqs.why: By the converse of Pythagoras' theorem, the square of the longest side must equal the sum of the squares of the other two. Full working: 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5², so 3, 4, 5 is right-angled.

mcqs.q: Each side of an equilateral triangle measures 8 cm. Find the length of its altitude.
mcqs.why: The altitude bisects the base, so half the base is 4 cm. Full working: (altitude)² = 8² − 4² = 64 − 16 = 48, so altitude = √48 = 4√3 cm ≈ 6.93 cm.

mcqs.q: The base of an isosceles triangle is 10 cm and the perpendicular from the vertex to the base is 12 cm. Find each congruent side.
mcqs.why: The perpendicular bisects the base, so each half is 5 cm. Full working: (side)² = 12² + 5² = 144 + 25 = 169, so each congruent side = √169 = 13 cm.

mcqs.q: In quadrilateral ABCD the diagonals are perpendicular to each other. Which equality is proved in this exercise?
mcqs.why: Applying Pythagoras' theorem in the four right triangles formed at the intersection E gives AB² + CD² = AE² + BE² + CE² + DE² and AD² + BC² = the same sum, so AB² + CD² = AD² + BC².

mcqs.q: The sides of a triangle are x, x + 4 and 20, with 20 the longest side. What value of x makes it a right triangle?
mcqs.why: Full working: x² + (x + 4)² = 20² gives x² + x² + 8x + 16 = 400, so 2x² + 8x − 384 = 0, i.e. x² + 4x − 192 = 0 = (x + 16)(x − 12). Hence x = 12; x = −16 is rejected as a length cannot be negative.

mcqs.q: With x = 12, what are the three sides of the right triangle in the previous type of problem (sides x, x + 4, 20)?
mcqs.why: Substituting x = 12: the sides are x = 12, x + 4 = 16 and 20. Check: 12² + 16² = 144 + 256 = 400 = 20², confirming a right triangle with sides 12, 16 and 20.

mcqs.q: In the equilateral triangle altitude problem (side 8 cm), why is 4 cm used in the Pythagoras calculation?
options: It is the perimeter divided by 4
The altitude bisects the base, so half the base is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm
mcqs.why: The altitude of an equilateral triangle falls on the midpoint of the base, splitting the 8 cm base into two parts of 4 cm each. That half-base, with the side 8 cm as hypotenuse, gives altitude² = 8² − 4² = 48.

mcqs.q: In the isosceles triangle problem (base 10 cm, perpendicular 12 cm), what length is half the base?
mcqs.why: The perpendicular from the vertex of an isosceles triangle bisects the base. Half the base is therefore 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm, and this 5 cm is used with the 12 cm perpendicular to get the congruent side of 13 cm.

mcqs.q: What is the converse of Pythagoras' theorem used to test whether a triangle is right-angled?
options: If c² = a² + b² then the triangle is equilateral
If the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, the triangle is right-angled
Every triangle with sides in ratio 3:4:5 is isosceles
If a² + b² > c² the triangle is right-angled
mcqs.why: The converse states: if the square of the longest side of a triangle equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, then the triangle is right-angled. This is exactly the test applied to triples such as 3, 4, 5 in this review.

lessons.title: Exercise 16.1
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Triangles on the same base and between the same parallels are equal in area, because they have the same base and the same altitude.
  • In △ABC with PQ ∥ BC, △PBC and △QBC are equal in area because they stand on the same base BC between the parallels PQ and BC.
  • Subtracting a common part preserves equality of area: since △PBC = △QBC, removing the common △RBC gives △BRP = △CRQ.
  • Adding a common part also preserves equality: since △PQB = △PQC (same base PQ), adding the common △APQ gives △ABQ = △ACP.
  • In parallelogram PQRS with A and B the midpoints of PQ and PS, △PAB is 1/8, △QBR is 1/2 and △BAR is 3/8 of the area of the parallelogram.
  • If two triangles on the same base AD have equal areas (△ABD = △ACD), their vertices B and C are at equal distances from AD, so AD ∥ BC.
  • Number of 8-inch square tiles for an 18 ft by 30 ft floor: floor area 540 × 144 = 77,760 sq in, tile area 64 sq in, so 77,760 ÷ 64 = 1215 tiles.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). In △ABC, PQ is drawn parallel to BC, cutting AB and AC at points P and Q respectively. BQ and CP are drawn to meet at R. Prove that the following are equal in areas: △PBC and △QBC.

Ans: Given:
In △ABC, P is a point on AB and Q is a point on AC with PQ ∥ BC. Segments BQ and CP are drawn and meet at R inside the triangle.
To Prove:
Area of △PBC = Area of △QBC
Construction:
None.
Proof:
△PBC and △QBC stand on the same base BC — statement
Their vertices P and Q lie on the line PQ, which is parallel to BC — statement (given)
∴ the two triangles have the same altitude — reason: triangles on the same base and between the same parallels have equal altitudes
∴ Area of △PBC = Area of △QBC — reason: triangles on the same base and between the same parallels are equal in area
Hence proved.

Q: Q1(ii). In △ABC, PQ is drawn parallel to BC, cutting AB and AC at points P and Q respectively. BQ and CP are drawn to meet at R. Prove that the following are equal in areas: △BRP and △CRQ.

Ans: Given:
In △ABC, P is a point on AB and Q is a point on AC with PQ ∥ BC. Segments BQ and CP meet at R.
To Prove:
Area of △BRP = Area of △CRQ
Construction:
None.
Proof:
Area of △PBC = Area of △QBC — reason: proved in part (i) (same base BC, between the same parallels PQ and BC)
△RBC is a common part of both triangles — statement
Subtracting: Area of △PBC − Area of △RBC = Area of △QBC − Area of △RBC — statement
But △PBC − △RBC = △BRP and △QBC − △RBC = △CRQ — statement
∴ Area of △BRP = Area of △CRQ
Hence proved.

Q: Q1(iii). In △ABC, PQ is drawn parallel to BC, cutting AB and AC at points P and Q respectively. BQ and CP are drawn to meet at R. Prove that the following are equal in areas: △PQB and △PQC.

Ans: Given:
In △ABC, P is a point on AB and Q is a point on AC with PQ ∥ BC. Segments BQ and CP meet at R.
To Prove:
Area of △PQB = Area of △PQC
Construction:
None.
Proof:
△PQB and △PQC stand on the same base PQ — statement
Their vertices B and C lie on the line BC, which is parallel to PQ — statement (given)
∴ the two triangles have the same altitude — reason: the distance between the parallel lines PQ and BC is constant
∴ Area of △PQB = Area of △PQC — reason: triangles on the same base and between the same parallels are equal in area
Hence proved.

Q: Q1(iv). In △ABC, PQ is drawn parallel to BC, cutting AB and AC at points P and Q respectively. BQ and CP are drawn to meet at R. Prove that the following are equal in areas: △ABQ and △ACP.

Ans: Given:
In △ABC, P is a point on AB and Q is a point on AC with PQ ∥ BC. Segments BQ and CP meet at R.
To Prove:
Area of △ABQ = Area of △ACP
Construction:
None.
Proof:
Area of △PQB = Area of △PQC — reason: proved in part (iii) (same base PQ, between the same parallels)
△APQ is a common part: △ABQ = △APQ + △PQB and △ACP = △APQ + △PQC — statement
Adding the common area △APQ to the two equal areas of part (iii):
∴ Area of △ABQ = Area of △ACP
Hence proved.

Q: Q2. PQRS is a parallelogram. A and B are the mid points of PQ and PS respectively. What fraction of the area of the parallelogram is: i) △PAB ii) △QBR iii) △BAR

Ans: Let the area of parallelogram PQRS be denoted by S, with base PQ and altitude h, so S = PQ × h.
i) △PAB has base PA = (1/2)PQ (A is the midpoint of PQ), and its vertex B is the midpoint of PS, so the altitude of △PAB from B to the line PQ is (1/2)h.
Area of △PAB = (1/2) × (1/2)PQ × (1/2)h = (1/8)PQ × h = S/8
ii) Joining B to Q and R splits the parallelogram into △PQB, △QBR and △BRS (B lies on side PS).
Area of △PQB = (1/2) × PQ × (h/2) = S/4 (base PQ; B, the midpoint of PS, is at half the altitude, h/2, above PQ).
Area of △BRS = (1/2) × RS × (h/2) = S/4 (base RS = PQ; B is at distance h/2 below the line RS).
Area of △QBR = S − S/4 − S/4 = S/2
iii) △BAR: A is the midpoint of PQ and B the midpoint of PS. Area(△BAR) = S − Area(△PAB) − Area(△AQR) − Area(△BRS). Area(△PAB) = S/8 (part i). Area(△AQR): base AQ = (1/2)PQ, altitude from R to line PQ is h, so area = (1/2)(PQ/2)h = S/4. Area(△BRS): base BS = (1/2)PS, altitude from R to line PS equals the distance between the parallels QR and PS... = (1/2)(PS/2) × (distance) where (1/2) × PS × distance = S, so Area(△BRS) = S/4.
Area(△BAR) = S − S/8 − S/4 − S/4 = S − 5S/8 = 3S/8
Answer: i) △PAB is 1/8 of the area of the parallelogram. ii) △QBR is 1/2 of the area of the parallelogram. iii) △BAR is 3/8 of the area of the parallelogram.

Q: Q3. ABCD is a quadrilateral. The diagonals AC and BD meet at E. If △ABE and △CDE are equal in area then prove that AD ∥ BC.

Ans: Given:
ABCD is a quadrilateral whose diagonals AC and BD intersect at E. Area of △ABE = Area of △CDE.
To Prove:
AD ∥ BC
Construction:
None.
Proof:
Area of △ABE = Area of △CDE — statement (given)
Add Area of △AED to both sides: Area of △ABE + Area of △AED = Area of △CDE + Area of △AED — statement
But △ABE + △AED = △ABD and △CDE + △AED = △ACD — statement
∴ Area of △ABD = Area of △ACD — statement
△ABD and △ACD stand on the same base AD — statement
Two triangles on the same base with equal areas have equal altitudes, so their vertices B and C are at the same distance from the line AD — reason: area = (1/2) × base × altitude
∴ B and C lie on a line parallel to AD — reason: points at equal perpendicular distances from a line, on the same side, lie on a line parallel to it
∴ AD ∥ BC
Hence proved.

Q: Q4. A floor is covered with tiles that are 8 inches square. If the floor is 18 feet by 30 feet, how many tiles are needed to cover the floor?

Ans: Area of the floor = 18 ft × 30 ft = 540 square feet.
Convert to square inches: 1 square foot = 144 square inches, so area = 540 × 144 = 77,760 square inches.
Area of one tile = 8 in × 8 in = 64 square inches.
Number of tiles = 77,760 ÷ 64 = 1215
Check by lengths: along 18 ft = 216 in need 216 ÷ 8 = 27 tiles; along 30 ft = 360 in need 360 ÷ 8 = 45 tiles; total = 27 × 45 = 1215 tiles.
Answer: 1215 tiles are needed.
Note: The book's printed answer is incorrect; the correct answer is 1215 (the key divided the area by the side length 8 instead of by the tile area 64).

mcqs.q: Triangles on the same base and between the same parallels are:
mcqs.why: Triangles on the same base and between the same parallels have the same base and the same altitude (the distance between the parallels), so by area = (1/2) × base × altitude their areas are equal.

mcqs.q: In △ABC, PQ ∥ BC. Why are △PBC and △QBC equal in area?
options: They stand on the same base BC and between the same parallels PQ and BC
mcqs.why: Both triangles stand on the same base BC, and their vertices P and Q lie on the line PQ which is parallel to BC. Same base and same altitude means equal areas, so area of △PBC = area of △QBC.

mcqs.q: Given area of △PBC = area of △QBC, with BQ and CP meeting at R, how is area of △BRP = area of △CRQ obtained?
options: By adding the common △RBC to both
By subtracting the common △RBC from both equal areas
mcqs.why: △RBC is a common part of both △PBC and △QBC. Subtracting equals from equals gives equals: △PBC − △RBC = △BRP and △QBC − △RBC = △CRQ, so the two remaining triangles are equal in area.

mcqs.q: In △ABC with PQ ∥ BC, △PQB and △PQC are equal in area because they stand on:
options: The same base PQ, between the parallels PQ and BC
The same base BC, between the parallels AB and AC
The base AB with a common vertex
mcqs.why: △PQB and △PQC share the same base PQ, while their vertices B and C lie on BC, which is parallel to PQ. The distance between the parallels is constant, so the altitudes are equal and the areas are equal.

mcqs.q: Given area of △PQB = area of △PQC, how is area of △ABQ = area of △ACP proved?
options: By applying the converse of Pythagoras' theorem
By adding the common △APQ to both equal areas
mcqs.why: △APQ is common: △ABQ = △APQ + △PQB and △ACP = △APQ + △PQC. Adding the same area △APQ to the two equal areas of △PQB and △PQC gives area of △ABQ = area of △ACP.

mcqs.q: PQRS is a parallelogram and A and B are the midpoints of PQ and PS. What fraction of the parallelogram is △PAB?
mcqs.why: Let the parallelogram have area S = PQ × h. △PAB has base PA = (1/2)PQ and altitude (1/2)h from B. Area = (1/2) × (1/2)PQ × (1/2)h = (1/8)PQ × h = S/8, i.e. 1/8 of the parallelogram.

mcqs.q: With the same parallelogram PQRS and midpoints A and B, what fraction of the parallelogram is △QBR?
mcqs.why: Full working: △PQB = (1/2) × PQ × (h/2) = S/4 and △BRS = S/4 by the same reasoning. So △QBR = S − S/4 − S/4 = S/2, i.e. 1/2 of the area of the parallelogram.

mcqs.q: With the same parallelogram PQRS and midpoints A and B, what fraction of the parallelogram is △BAR?
mcqs.why: Full working: △BAR = S − △PAB − △AQR − △BRS = S − S/8 − S/4 − S/4 = S − 5S/8 = 3S/8, so △BAR is 3/8 of the area of the parallelogram.

mcqs.q: In quadrilateral ABCD, the diagonals meet at E and area of △ABE = area of △CDE. Adding area of △AED to both sides gives which equality, used to prove AD ∥ BC?
mcqs.why: Adding the common △AED: △ABE + △AED = △ABD and △CDE + △AED = △ACD, so area of △ABD = area of △ACD. These stand on the same base AD with equal areas, hence equal altitudes, which gives AD ∥ BC.

mcqs.q: A floor 18 feet by 30 feet is covered with tiles 8 inches square. How many tiles are needed?
mcqs.why: Full working: floor area = 18 × 30 = 540 sq ft = 540 × 144 = 77,760 sq in. One tile has area 8 × 8 = 64 sq in. Number of tiles = 77,760 ÷ 64 = 1215. Check by lengths: 27 × 45 = 1215 tiles.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 16
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • If the perpendicular distance between two lines is the same everywhere, the lines are parallel to each other.
  • Two triangles with equal area are not necessarily congruent; equal area does not imply equal sides and angles.
  • The perpendicular from a vertex of a triangle to its opposite side is called the altitude of the triangle.
  • Parallelograms having the same base and the same altitude are equal in area (they are not necessarily congruent).
  • Two parallelograms with equal bases have the same area when their altitudes are equal, i.e. when they lie between the same parallel lines.
  • If two triangles have equal bases and equal altitudes, they have equal areas, since area = (1/2) × base × altitude.
  • The median of a triangle divides it into two triangles of equal area, because the two parts have equal bases and the same altitude.
  • Area calculations from this review: base 4 ft and height 4 ft give 8 sq ft; a square with diagonal 10 has area 50; base 20 in and altitude 12 in give 120 sq in.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Perpendicular distance between two lines is the same. The lines are

Options: (a) Perpendicular to each other (b) Parallel to each other (c) Intersecting (d) None of the above

Correct answer: Parallel to each other

Q: Q1(ii). If two triangles have equal area then they will ________ be congruent as well.

Options: (a) Not necessarily (b) Necessarily (c) Definitely (d) None of the above

Correct answer: Not necessarily

Q: Q1(iii). Perpendicular from a vertex of a triangle to its opposite side is called ________.

Options: (a) Median (b) Perpendicular bisector (c) Altitude (d) Angle bisector

Correct answer: Altitude

Q: Q1(iv). Parallelograms having same base and same altitude are ________.

Options: (a) Congruent (b) Equal in area (c) Similar (d) All of the above

Correct answer: Equal in area

Q: Q1(v). Two parallelograms have equal bases. They will be having the same area if ________.

Options: (a) Their altitudes are equal (b) Their altitude is the same (c) They lie between the same parallel lines (d) All of the above

Correct answer: All of the above

Q: Q1(vi). If two triangles have equal bases and equal altitudes, what else will they have equal?

Options: (a) area (b) perimeter (c) size (d) angles

Correct answer: area

Q: Q1(vii). Suppose a triangle has a base length of 4 feet and a height of 4 feet. Its interior area is

Options: (a) 4 square feet (b) 8 square feet (c) 16 square feet (d) Impossible to determine without more information

Correct answer: 8 square feet

Q: Q1(viii). Suppose a square has a diagonal measure of 10 units. The area of the square is

Options: (a) 25 square feet (b) 50 square feet (c) 100 square feet (d) Impossible to determine without more information

Correct answer: 50 square feet

Q: Q1(ix). Find the area of a triangle with base 15/4 inches and altitude 8/5 inches.

Options: (a) 2 sq. in (b) 6 sq. in (c) 3 sq. in (d) 4.35 sq. in

Correct answer: 3 sq. in

Q: Q2. Prove that the median of a triangle divides it into two triangles of equal area.

Ans: Given:
In △ABC, D is the midpoint of BC and AD is a median.
To Prove:
Area of △ABD = Area of △ACD
Construction:
Draw AE perpendicular to BC, with E on BC.
Proof:
BD = DC — reason: D is the midpoint of BC (given)
Area of △ABD = (1/2) × BD × AE — reason: area = (1/2) × base × altitude, with common altitude AE
Area of △ACD = (1/2) × DC × AE — reason: same altitude AE
Since BD = DC, the two areas are equal
∴ Area of △ABD = Area of △ACD
Hence the median divides the triangle into two triangles of equal area.
Hence proved.

Q: Q3. In △ABC, D and E are the mid points of AB and AC respectively. Prove that △ADE, △BDE and △CDE are equal in area.

Ans: Given:
In △ABC, D is the midpoint of AB and E is the midpoint of AC.
To Prove:
Area of △ADE = Area of △BDE = Area of △CDE
Construction:
None.
Proof:
DE ∥ BC — reason: the segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side (midsegment theorem)
△BDE and △CDE stand on the same base DE and between the same parallels DE and BC — statement
∴ Area of △BDE = Area of △CDE — reason: triangles on the same base and between the same parallels are equal in area
△ADE and △BDE stand on equal bases AD = DB on the same line AB and have the same altitude from E — statement (D is the midpoint of AB)
∴ Area of △ADE = Area of △BDE — reason: triangles with equal bases and the same altitude are equal in area
∴ Area of △ADE = Area of △BDE = Area of △CDE
Hence proved.

Q: Q4. P is any point on the median AD of △ABC. Prove that △ABP and △ACP are equal in area.

Ans: Given:
In △ABC, AD is a median, so D is the midpoint of BC. P is any point on the median AD.
To Prove:
Area of △ABP = Area of △ACP
Construction:
None.
Proof:
Area of △ABD = Area of △ACD — reason: a median divides a triangle into two triangles of equal area (AD is a median of △ABC)
PD is a median of △PBC — reason: D is the midpoint of BC
∴ Area of △PBD = Area of △PCD — reason: a median divides a triangle into two triangles of equal area
Subtracting: Area of △ABD − Area of △PBD = Area of △ACD − Area of △PCD — statement
But △ABD − △PBD = △ABP and △ACD − △PCD = △ACP — statement
∴ Area of △ABP = Area of △ACP
Hence proved.

Q: Q5. Find the area of a triangle with base 20 inches and altitude 12 inches.

Ans: Area of a triangle = (1/2) × base × altitude.
Area = (1/2) × 20 × 12
= 10 × 12
= 120 square inches
Answer: The area of the triangle is 120 sq. inches.

Q: Note

Ans: For Q1(iv) above: the book's printed answer key gives (d) All of the above, which is incorrect — parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels are equal in area, but they are not necessarily congruent. The correct option is (b) Equal.

mcqs.q: The perpendicular distance between two lines is the same everywhere. The lines are:
mcqs.why: A constant perpendicular distance between two lines means the lines never meet and stay the same distance apart, which is the defining property of parallel lines. Intersecting or perpendicular lines have varying distance.

mcqs.q: If two triangles have equal area, then they will ________ be congruent as well.
mcqs.why: Equal area only fixes (1/2) × base × altitude; many different shapes share the same area. So two triangles of equal area are not necessarily congruent — their sides and angles may all differ.

mcqs.q: The perpendicular from a vertex of a triangle to its opposite side is called the ________.
mcqs.why: By definition, the perpendicular drawn from a vertex to the opposite side (or its extension) is the altitude. A median joins a vertex to the midpoint, and an angle bisector halves an angle, so neither is correct.

mcqs.q: Parallelograms having the same base and the same altitude are ________.
mcqs.why: Area of a parallelogram = base × altitude. With the same base and the same altitude the areas must be equal. They need not be congruent, because the slant (angles) can differ while base and altitude stay the same.

mcqs.q: Two parallelograms have equal bases. They will have the same area if ________.
options: Their altitudes are equal, so they lie between the same parallel lines
mcqs.why: Area = base × altitude. With equal bases, the areas are equal exactly when the altitudes are equal, which is the same as the parallelograms lying between the same pair of parallel lines.

mcqs.q: If two triangles have equal bases and equal altitudes, what else will they have equal?
mcqs.why: Area of a triangle = (1/2) × base × altitude. If both the base and the altitude are equal for two triangles, then (1/2) × base × altitude is the same for both, so their areas are equal.

mcqs.q: A triangle has base 4 feet and height 4 feet. Its area is:
mcqs.why: Full working: area = (1/2) × base × height = (1/2) × 4 × 4 = (1/2) × 16 = 8 square feet. The factor 1/2 must not be forgotten.

mcqs.q: A square has a diagonal of 10 units. The area of the square is:
mcqs.why: Full working: for a square, diagonal² = side² + side² = 2 × area, so area = diagonal² ÷ 2 = 10² ÷ 2 = 100 ÷ 2 = 50 square units.

mcqs.q: Find the area of a triangle with base 15/4 inches and altitude 8/5 inches.
Find the area of a triangle with base 20 inches and altitude 12 inches.
mcqs.why: Full working: area = (1/2) × base × altitude = (1/2) × 20 × 12 = 10 × 12 = 120 square inches, as worked in Q5 of this review exercise.

lessons.title: Exercise 17.1
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • S.A.S construction: draw one side with the ruler, construct the given included angle at its endpoint, cut off the second side along the new arm with the compass, and join the endpoints; two sides and the included angle determine a unique triangle.
  • A.S.A construction: draw the given side, construct the two given angles at its two endpoints on the same side, and extend the arms until they meet at the third vertex; a side and its two adjacent angles determine a unique triangle.
  • If a side and two angles are given but the angles are not both at the endpoints of the side, first find the third angle from 180° minus the sum of the two given angles, then use A.S.A at the endpoints of the side.
  • Examples of the third-angle step: angles 45° and 60° give a third angle of 75°; angles 30° and 60° give a third angle of 90°, so the triangle is right-angled.
  • S.S.A is the ambiguous case: with a given angle, an adjacent side and the opposite side, the number of triangles depends on comparing the opposite side with the perpendicular distance (adjacent side × sin of the given angle).
  • In the S.S.A case, if the opposite side exactly equals the perpendicular distance, the arc is tangent to the base line and exactly one triangle can be drawn (right-angled), e.g. AB = 8 cm, angle B = 30°, AC = 4 cm = 8 × sin 30°.
  • In the S.S.A case, if the opposite side lies between the perpendicular distance and the adjacent side, the arc cuts the base line at two points and two triangles can be drawn, e.g. 4.95 < 5.5 < 7 and 5.20 < 5.6 < 6 in the exercise.
  • Every S.A.S and A.S.A construction in this exercise gives exactly one triangle; only the S.S.A data can give zero, one or two triangles.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Construct a △XYZ for the following assumptions: m∠X = 30°, mXY = 3.5 cm and mXZ = 4 cm

Ans: Given:
m∠X = 30°, mXY = 3.5 cm and mXZ = 4 cm; the angle at X is included between XY and XZ.
Required:
Construct △XYZ.
Diagram: The finished figure is △XYZ with X at the left, XY = 3.5 cm along the base, XZ = 4 cm rising from X at 30° to XY, Z at the top and Y at the right, with Z joined to Y.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the line segment XY = 3.5 cm with the ruler.
(ii) At the vertex of the given angle, construct the angle of 30° at X.
(iii) Along the new arm, cut off XZ = 4 cm with the compass.
(iv) Join the endpoints to complete the triangle and label all vertices and measures.
Justification:
Two sides and the included angle (S.A.S) determine a unique triangle, so the construction gives exactly △XYZ.

Q: Q3(i). Construct a △KLM for the following assumptions: mKL = 4.8 cm, m∠K = 45° and m∠M = 60°

Ans: Given:
mKL = 4.8 cm, m∠K = 45° and m∠M = 60°; the third angle is m∠L = 180° − 45° − 60° = 75°, so the side KL has the angles 45° (at K) and 75° (at L) at its endpoints.
Required:

Diagram: The finished figure is △KLM with base KL = 4.8 cm, M above the base where the 45° arm from K and the 75° arm from L meet (check: the angle at M measures 60°).
Steps of Construction:

(ii) At its two endpoints, construct the angle of 45° at K and the angle of 75° at L (computed as 180° − 45° − 60°) on the same side of the segment.
(iii) Extend the two new arms until they meet at the third vertex.

The two given angles fix the third angle, so a side with its two endpoint angles (A.S.A) determines a unique triangle.

Required:

Steps of Construction:

Q: Q4(i). Construct a △ABC (whenever possible) for the following assumptions: m∠B = 30°, mAB = 8 cm and mAC = 4 cm

Ans: Given:
m∠B = 30°, mAB = 8 cm (a side adjacent to ∠B) and mAC = 4 cm (the side opposite ∠B) — the ambiguous S.S.A case.
Required:
Construct △ABC if possible and state how many such triangles can be drawn.
Diagram: The finished figure is a single △ABC, right-angled at C, with B at the left, BA = 8 cm along the base line, the 30° angle at B, and C the foot of the perpendicular from A, with AC = 4 cm.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw a line and mark B on it; construct the angle of 30° at B.
(ii) Along the upper arm cut off BA = 8 cm.
(iii) From A drop a perpendicular to the base line; its length is AB sin 30° = 8 × 0.5 = 4 cm.
(iv) The given side AC = 4 cm exactly equals this perpendicular distance, so the arc of radius 4 cm centred at A just touches the base line at one point, C.
(v) Join A to C to complete the single triangle.
Justification:
In the S.S.A case the number of triangles depends on the side opposite the given angle compared with the perpendicular distance AB sin B = 4 cm. Here AC = 4 cm equals that distance, so the arc is tangent to the base line and exactly ONE triangle can be drawn (it is right-angled at C).

Q: Q4(ii). Construct a △ABC (whenever possible) for the following assumptions: mAB = 7 cm, mAC = 5.5 cm and m∠B = 45°

Ans: Given:
mAB = 7 cm (a side adjacent to ∠B), mAC = 5.5 cm (the side opposite ∠B) and m∠B = 45° — the ambiguous S.S.A case.
Required:
Construct △ABC if possible and state how many such triangles can be drawn.
Diagram: The finished figure shows two different triangles with the same data: △ABC₁ and △ABC₂, with C₁ and C₂ two distinct points on the base line, both joined to A and B.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw a line and mark B on it; construct the angle of 45° at B.
(ii) Along the upper arm cut off BA = 7 cm.
(iii) The perpendicular distance from A to the base line is AB sin 45° = 7 × 0.707 ≈ 4.95 cm.
(iv) With centre A and radius AC = 5.5 cm draw an arc; since 4.95 < 5.5 < 7, the arc cuts the base line at two distinct points C₁ and C₂.
(v) Join A to C₁ and A to C₂ to obtain the two triangles.
Justification:
In the S.S.A case, when the side opposite the given angle (5.5 cm) lies between the perpendicular distance (≈ 4.95 cm) and the adjacent side AB (7 cm), the arc cuts the base line twice, so TWO triangles can be drawn.

Justification:

Q: Q7. Construct △KLM such that mKL = 4.8 cm, mLM = 3.9 cm and m∠L = 30°. (This question is printed without a number, between Q6 and Q8.)

Ans: Given:
mKL = 4.8 cm, mLM = 3.9 cm and m∠L = 30°; the angle at L is included between KL and LM.
Required:
Construct △KLM.
Diagram: The finished figure is △KLM with L at the left, KL = 4.8 cm along the base to K at the right, LM = 3.9 cm rising from L at 30°, M at the top, and M joined to K.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the line segment KL = 4.8 cm with the ruler.
(ii) At the vertex of the given angle, construct the angle of 30° at L.
(iii) Along the new arm, cut off LM = 3.9 cm with the compass.
(iv) Join the endpoints to complete the triangle and label all vertices and measures.
Justification:
Two sides and the included angle (S.A.S) determine a unique triangle.

Q: Q8. Construct △PQR such that mQR = 6.5 cm, m∠P = 30° and m∠Q = 60°

Ans: Given:
mQR = 6.5 cm, m∠P = 30° and m∠Q = 60°; the third angle is m∠R = 180° − 30° − 60° = 90°, so the side QR has the angles 60° (at Q) and 90° (at R) at its endpoints.
Required:
Construct △PQR.
Diagram: The finished figure is △PQR right-angled at R, with QR = 6.5 cm along the base, R at the right, PR vertical at R, P at the top and Q at the left (check: the angle at P measures 30°).
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the line segment QR = 6.5 cm with the ruler.
(ii) At its two endpoints, construct the angle of 60° at Q and the right angle of 90° at R (computed as 180° − 30° − 60°) on the same side of the segment.
(iii) Extend the two new arms until they meet at the third vertex.
(iv) Label all vertices and measures.
Justification:
The two given angles fix the third angle, so a side with its two endpoint angles (A.S.A) determines a unique triangle.

lessons.title: Exercise 17.2
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • S.S.S construction: draw one side, then draw arcs with compass radii equal to the other two sides from its two endpoints; their intersection is the third vertex, and three sides determine a unique triangle.
  • Angle bisector construction: place the compass point on the vertex, draw an arc cutting both arms, then draw equal arcs from the two cutting points meeting inside the angle, and join the vertex to the meeting point.
  • The three angle bisectors of a triangle are concurrent at one interior point, the incentre, as verified in Q1 of this exercise.
  • Altitude construction: from a vertex, draw an arc cutting the opposite side (produced if necessary) at two points, draw equal arcs from those points, and join the vertex to their meeting point; the line is perpendicular to the opposite side.
  • The three altitudes of a triangle are concurrent at the orthocentre, as verified in Q2 of this exercise.
  • Perpendicular bisector construction: with radius more than half the side, draw arcs above and below the side from both endpoints and join the two meeting points; every point on it is equidistant from the side's endpoints.
  • The three perpendicular bisectors of a triangle are concurrent at the circumcentre; for an obtuse triangle this point lies outside the triangle, as in Q3(ii).
  • Median construction: find the midpoint of a side by the compass bisection construction and join it to the opposite vertex; the three medians are concurrent at the centroid, as verified in Q4. In an equilateral triangle the angle bisectors, altitudes, perpendicular bisectors and medians coincide, so all four concurrency points are the same central point.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Construct △ABC, draw their angle bisectors and verify their concurrency: mAB = 4.5 cm, mBC = 3.1 cm and mCA = 5.2 cm

Ans: Given:
mAB = 4.5 cm, mBC = 3.1 cm and mCA = 5.2 cm — the three sides of △ABC.
Required:
Construct △ABC, draw the bisectors of its angles and verify that they are concurrent.
Diagram: The finished figure is △ABC with base AB = 4.5 cm, C above the base with CA = 5.2 cm and CB = 3.1 cm; the bisectors from A, B and C meet at one interior point.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the line segment AB = 4.5 cm with the ruler.
(ii) With the compass centred at one endpoint and radius 5.2 cm (for CA, from A), draw an arc above the segment.
(iii) With the compass centred at the other endpoint and radius 3.1 cm (for CB, from B), draw a second arc cutting the first arc.
(iv) Join the intersection point of the arcs to both endpoints and label all vertices and measures.
(v) Draw the bisector of each angle: place the compass point on the vertex, draw an arc cutting both arms; from the two cutting points draw equal arcs meeting inside the angle; join the vertex to the meeting point.
(vi) The three bisectors are seen to meet at one point — their concurrency is verified.
Justification:
Three sides (S.S.S) determine a unique triangle. Each bisector is drawn by the equal-arcs construction: the two small triangles formed on either side of the ray are congruent by S.S.S, so the ray halves the angle. The three angle bisectors of a triangle are concurrent (at the incentre), as verified in the figure.

Q: Q1(ii). Construct △ABC, draw their angle bisectors and verify their concurrency: mAB = mBC = mCA = 12

Ans: Given:
mAB = mBC = mCA = 12 (units) — an equilateral triangle.
Required:
Construct △ABC, draw the bisectors of its angles and verify that they are concurrent.
Diagram: The finished figure is the equilateral △ABC with all sides 12; the three angle bisectors meet at the centre of the triangle (each is also a median, altitude and perpendicular bisector).
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the line segment AB = 12 with the ruler.
(ii) With the compass centred at one endpoint and radius 12 (for CA, from A), draw an arc above the segment.
(iii) With the compass centred at the other endpoint and radius 12 (for CB, from B), draw a second arc cutting the first arc.
(iv) Join the intersection point of the arcs to both endpoints and label all vertices and measures.
(v) Draw the bisector of each angle: place the compass point on the vertex, draw an arc cutting both arms; from the two cutting points draw equal arcs meeting inside the angle; join the vertex to the meeting point.
(vi) The three bisectors are seen to meet at one point — their concurrency is verified.
Justification:
Three sides (S.S.S) determine a unique triangle; with all sides equal it is equilateral, so all angles are 60°. Each bisector is drawn by the equal-arcs construction: the two small triangles formed on either side of the ray are congruent by S.S.S, so the ray halves the angle. The three angle bisectors of a triangle are concurrent (at the incentre), as verified in the figure.

Q: Q1(iii). Construct △ABC, draw their angle bisectors and verify their concurrency: mCA = 5.8 cm, m∠A = 45° and m∠C = 75°

Ans: Given:
mCA = 5.8 cm, m∠A = 45° and m∠C = 75°; the side CA is included between the angles at A and C (the third angle at B is 60°).
Required:
Construct △ABC, draw the bisectors of its angles and verify that they are concurrent.
Diagram: The finished figure is △ABC with base CA = 5.8 cm, B above the base; the bisectors from A, B and C meet at one interior point.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the line segment CA = 5.8 cm with the ruler.
(ii) At its two endpoints, construct the angle of 45° at A and the angle of 75° at C on the same side of the segment.
(iii) Extend the two new arms until they meet at the third vertex.
(iv) Label all vertices and measures.
(v) Draw the bisector of each angle: place the compass point on the vertex, draw an arc cutting both arms; from the two cutting points draw equal arcs meeting inside the angle; join the vertex to the meeting point.
(vi) The three bisectors are seen to meet at one point — their concurrency is verified.
Justification:
A side and its two adjacent angles (A.S.A) determine a unique triangle. Each bisector is drawn by the equal-arcs construction: the two small triangles formed on either side of the ray are congruent by S.S.S, so the ray halves the angle. The three angle bisectors of a triangle are concurrent (at the incentre), as verified in the figure.

Q: Q2(i). Construct △PQR, draw their altitudes and verify their concurrency: mPQ = 6 cm, mQR = 4.5 cm and mPR = 5.5 cm

Ans: Given:
mPQ = 6 cm, mQR = 4.5 cm and mPR = 5.5 cm — the three sides of △PQR.
Required:
Construct △PQR, draw its altitudes and verify that they are concurrent.
Diagram: The finished figure is △PQR with base PQ = 6 cm, R above the base with PR = 5.5 cm and QR = 4.5 cm; the altitudes from P, Q and R meet at one interior point.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the line segment PQ = 6 cm with the ruler.
(ii) With the compass centred at one endpoint and radius 5.5 cm (for PR, from P), draw an arc above the segment.
(iii) With the compass centred at the other endpoint and radius 4.5 cm (for QR, from Q), draw a second arc cutting the first arc.
(iv) Join the intersection point of the arcs to both endpoints and label all vertices and measures.
(v) Draw the altitude from each vertex: place the compass point on the vertex, draw an arc cutting the opposite side (produced if necessary) at two points; from these points draw equal arcs meeting beyond the side; join the vertex to the meeting point — the line is perpendicular to the opposite side.
(vi) The three altitudes are seen to meet at one point — their concurrency is verified.
Justification:
Three sides (S.S.S) determine a unique triangle. Each altitude is drawn by the perpendicular-from-a-point construction, so it is perpendicular to the opposite side. The three altitudes of a triangle are concurrent (at the orthocentre), as verified in the figure.

Q: Q2(ii). Construct △PQR, draw their altitudes and verify their concurrency: mPQ = 4.5 cm, mQR = 3.9 cm and m∠R = 45°

Ans: Given:
mPQ = 4.5 cm, mQR = 3.9 cm and m∠R = 45°; the angle at R is included between QR and PR, with PR found by the construction (S.A.S form: draw QR, the 45° angle at R, and P on the arm at distance PQ = 4.5 cm from Q).
Required:
Construct △PQR, draw its altitudes and verify that they are concurrent.
Diagram: The finished figure is △PQR with QR = 3.9 cm, R at the right, the 45° angle at R, P above the base with PQ = 4.5 cm; the altitudes from P, Q and R meet at one point.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw QR = 3.9 cm.
(ii) At R construct the angle of 45° and draw the arm (P lies on this arm).
(iii) With centre Q and radius PQ = 4.5 cm, draw an arc cutting the arm at P.
(iv) Join P to Q and label the triangle.
(v) Draw the altitude from each vertex: place the compass point on the vertex, draw an arc cutting the opposite side (produced if necessary) at two points; from these points draw equal arcs meeting beyond the side; join the vertex to the meeting point — the line is perpendicular to the opposite side.
(vi) The three altitudes are seen to meet at one point — their concurrency is verified.
Justification:
The data fix the triangle uniquely: P must lie on the 45° arm from R and at distance 4.5 cm from Q, and the arc meets the arm in one point on the correct side. Each altitude is drawn by the perpendicular-from-a-point construction, so it is perpendicular to the opposite side. The three altitudes of a triangle are concurrent (at the orthocentre), as verified in the figure.

Q: Q2(iii). Construct △PQR, draw their altitudes and verify their concurrency: mPQ = 6 cm, m∠P = 75° and m∠Q = 60°

Ans: Given:
mPQ = 6 cm, m∠P = 75° and m∠Q = 60°; the side PQ is included between the angles at P and Q (the third angle at R is 45°).
Required:
Construct △PQR, draw its altitudes and verify that they are concurrent.
Diagram: The finished figure is △PQR with base PQ = 6 cm, R above the base; the altitudes from P, Q and R meet at one interior point.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the line segment PQ = 6 cm with the ruler.
(ii) At its two endpoints, construct the angle of 75° at P and the angle of 60° at Q on the same side of the segment.
(iii) Extend the two new arms until they meet at the third vertex.
(iv) Label all vertices and measures.
(v) Draw the altitude from each vertex: place the compass point on the vertex, draw an arc cutting the opposite side (produced if necessary) at two points; from these points draw equal arcs meeting beyond the side; join the vertex to the meeting point — the line is perpendicular to the opposite side.
(vi) The three altitudes are seen to meet at one point — their concurrency is verified.
Justification:
A side and its two adjacent angles (A.S.A) determine a unique triangle. Each altitude is drawn by the perpendicular-from-a-point construction, so it is perpendicular to the opposite side. The three altitudes of a triangle are concurrent (at the orthocentre), as verified in the figure.

Q: Q3(i). Construct △UVW, draw their perpendicular bisectors and verify their concurrency: mUV = 7 cm, mVW = 6.5 cm and mWU = 5.8 cm

Ans: Given:
mUV = 7 cm, mVW = 6.5 cm and mWU = 5.8 cm — the three sides of △UVW.
Required:
Construct △UVW, draw the perpendicular bisectors of its sides and verify that they are concurrent.
Diagram: The finished figure is △UVW with base UV = 7 cm, W above the base with WU = 5.8 cm and WV = 6.5 cm; the perpendicular bisectors of the three sides meet at one point.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the line segment UV = 7 cm with the ruler.
(ii) With the compass centred at one endpoint and radius 5.8 cm (for WU, from U), draw an arc above the segment.
(iii) With the compass centred at the other endpoint and radius 6.5 cm (for WV, from V), draw a second arc cutting the first arc.
(iv) Join the intersection point of the arcs to both endpoints and label all vertices and measures.
(v) Draw the perpendicular bisector of each side: with radius more than half the side, draw arcs above and below the side from both endpoints; join the two meeting points of the arcs.
(vi) The three perpendicular bisectors are seen to meet at one point — their concurrency is verified.
Justification:
Three sides (S.S.S) determine a unique triangle. Each perpendicular bisector is drawn by equal arcs from the endpoints of a side; every point on it is equidistant from the side's endpoints. The three perpendicular bisectors of a triangle are concurrent (at the circumcentre), as verified in the figure.

Q: Q3(ii). Construct △UVW, draw their perpendicular bisectors and verify their concurrency: mVW = 10 cm, mWU = 4.2 cm and m∠W = 120°

Ans: Given:
mVW = 10 cm, mWU = 4.2 cm and m∠W = 120°; the angle at W is included between VW and WU.
Required:
Construct △UVW, draw the perpendicular bisectors of its sides and verify that they are concurrent.
Diagram: The finished figure is △UVW with W at the left, WV = 10 cm and WU = 4.2 cm opening at the obtuse angle 120°, V joined to U; the perpendicular bisectors of the three sides meet at one point (outside the triangle, since it is obtuse).
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the line segment VW = 10 cm with the ruler.
(ii) At the vertex of the given angle, construct the angle of 120° at W.
(iii) Along the new arm, cut off WU = 4.2 cm with the compass.
(iv) Join the endpoints to complete the triangle and label all vertices and measures.
(v) Draw the perpendicular bisector of each side: with radius more than half the side, draw arcs above and below the side from both endpoints; join the two meeting points of the arcs.
(vi) The three perpendicular bisectors are seen to meet at one point — their concurrency is verified.
Justification:
Two sides and the included angle (S.A.S) determine a unique triangle. Each perpendicular bisector is drawn by equal arcs from the endpoints of a side; every point on it is equidistant from the side's endpoints. The three perpendicular bisectors of a triangle are concurrent (at the circumcentre), as verified in the figure.

Q: Q3(iii). Construct △UVW, draw their perpendicular bisectors and verify their concurrency: mUV = mVW = mWU = 0.8 m

Ans: Given:
mUV = mVW = mWU = 0.8 m — an equilateral triangle of side 0.8 m (drawn at a convenient scale, e.g. 0.8 m represented by 8 cm).
Required:
Construct △UVW, draw the perpendicular bisectors of its sides and verify that they are concurrent.
Diagram: The finished figure is the equilateral △UVW with all sides 0.8 m; the perpendicular bisectors of the three sides meet at the centre of the triangle (each is also an angle bisector, median and altitude).
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the line segment UV = 0.8 m with the ruler.
(ii) With the compass centred at one endpoint and radius 0.8 m (for WU, from U), draw an arc above the segment.
(iii) With the compass centred at the other endpoint and radius 0.8 m (for WV, from V), draw a second arc cutting the first arc.
(iv) Join the intersection point of the arcs to both endpoints and label all vertices and measures.
(v) Draw the perpendicular bisector of each side: with radius more than half the side, draw arcs above and below the side from both endpoints; join the two meeting points of the arcs.
(vi) The three perpendicular bisectors are seen to meet at one point — their concurrency is verified.
Justification:
Three sides (S.S.S) determine a unique triangle; with all sides equal it is equilateral. Each perpendicular bisector is drawn by equal arcs from the endpoints of a side; every point on it is equidistant from the side's endpoints. The three perpendicular bisectors of a triangle are concurrent (at the circumcentre), as verified in the figure.

Q: Q4(i). Construct △XYZ, draw their medians and verify their concurrency: mYZ = 4.1 cm, m∠Y = 60° and m∠X = 75°

Ans: Given:
mYZ = 4.1 cm, m∠Y = 60° and m∠X = 75°; the third angle is m∠Z = 180° − 60° − 75° = 45°, so the side YZ has the angles 60° (at Y) and 45° (at Z) at its endpoints.
Required:
Construct △XYZ, draw its medians and verify that they are concurrent.
Diagram: The finished figure is △XYZ with base YZ = 4.1 cm, X above the base; the medians from X, Y and Z to the midpoints of the opposite sides meet at one interior point.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the line segment YZ = 4.1 cm with the ruler.
(ii) At its two endpoints, construct the angle of 60° at Y and the angle of 45° at Z (computed as 180° − 60° − 75°) on the same side of the segment.
(iii) Extend the two new arms until they meet at the third vertex.
(iv) Label all vertices and measures.
(v) Find the midpoint of each side with the compass (arcs from both endpoints, as for a perpendicular bisector) and join it to the opposite vertex to draw the three medians.
(vi) The three medians are seen to meet at one point — their concurrency is verified.
Justification:
The two given angles fix the third angle, so a side with its two endpoint angles (A.S.A) determines a unique triangle. Each median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side, the midpoint being found by the compass bisection construction. The three medians of a triangle are concurrent (at the centroid), as verified in the figure.

Q: Q4(ii). Construct △XYZ, draw their medians and verify their concurrency: mZX = 4.3 cm, m∠X = 75° and m∠Y = 45°

mZX = 4.3 cm, m∠X = 75° and m∠Y = 45°; the third angle is m∠Z = 180° − 75° − 45° = 60°, so the side ZX has the angles 60° (at Z) and 75° (at X) at its endpoints.

(iii) Extend the two new arms until they meet at the third vertex.
(iv) Label all vertices and measures.
(v) Find the midpoint of each side with the compass (arcs from both endpoints, as for a perpendicular bisector) and join it to the opposite vertex to draw the three medians.

Q: Q4(iii). Construct △XYZ, draw their medians and verify their concurrency: mXY = 4.5 cm, mYZ = 3.4 cm and mZX = 5.6 cm

Ans: Given:
