lessons.title: Exercise 17.3
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • To construct a triangle equal in area to a quadrilateral: draw a diagonal, through the opposite vertex draw a line parallel to the diagonal meeting a produced side, and join — the new triangle equals the quadrilateral because triangles on the same base between the same parallels are equal in area.
  • A rectangle equal in area to a triangle has the triangle's base as its length and half the triangle's altitude (h/2) as its breadth, since base × (h/2) = (1/2) × base × h.
  • To construct a square equal in area to a rectangle: place the length and breadth end to end on one line, draw a semicircle on the whole as diameter, and erect a perpendicular at the junction point; this perpendicular is the side of the square.
  • The side of the square equal in area to a rectangle is the geometric mean of the rectangle's sides: side = √(l × b); for 5 cm by 3.5 cm it is √17.5 ≈ 4.18 cm, and for 4.5 cm by 2.2 cm it is √9.9 ≈ 3.15 cm with area 9.9 cm².
  • A square equal in area to the sum of two squares is built on the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the two given sides: for sides 3 cm and 4 cm, the hypotenuse is √(3² + 4²) = 5 cm and the square on it has area 25 cm² = 9 cm² + 16 cm².
  • To transform a triangle into an equal square, first build the rectangle equal in area to the triangle (base by h/2), then build the square equal in area to that rectangle by the semicircle geometric-mean construction.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. Draw a quadrilateral ABCD such that mAB = 3 cm, m∠B = 60°, m∠A = 120°, mBC = 3.5 cm and mAD = 4 cm. Construct a triangle equal in area to the quadrilateral ABCD.

Ans: Given:
Quadrilateral ABCD with AB = 3 cm, ∠A = 120°, ∠B = 60°, BC = 3.5 cm and AD = 4 cm.
Required:
Draw quadrilateral ABCD and construct a triangle equal in area to it.
Diagram: The finished figure is quadrilateral ABCD (A at the lower left, B at the lower right, C above B, D above A) with diagonal AC drawn, BC produced to E, DE parallel to AC, and △ABE, which equals the quadrilateral in area.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw AB = 3 cm.
(ii) At A construct the angle 120° and along its arm cut off AD = 4 cm.
(iii) At B construct the angle 60° and along its arm cut off BC = 3.5 cm.
(iv) Join C to D to complete quadrilateral ABCD.
(v) Draw the diagonal AC.
(vi) Through D draw a line parallel to AC, meeting BC produced at E.
(vii) Join A to E; △ABE is the required triangle.
Justification:
△ADC and △AEC stand on the same base AC and between the same parallels AC and DE, so they are equal in area. Adding △ABC to both: quadrilateral ABCD = △ADC + △ABC = △AEC + △ABC = △ABE. Hence △ABE is equal in area to quadrilateral ABCD.

Q: Q2. Draw a rectangle PQRS such that mPQ = 5 cm and mQR = 3.5 cm. Construct a square equal in area to rectangle PQRS.

Ans: Given:
Rectangle PQRS with PQ = 5 cm and QR = 3.5 cm; its area is 5 × 3.5 = 17.5 cm².
Required:
Draw rectangle PQRS and construct a square equal in area to it.
Diagram: The finished figure is the rectangle PQRS (5 cm by 3.5 cm) and a square of side √17.5 ≈ 4.18 cm, whose area is 17.5 cm².
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the rectangle PQRS with PQ = 5 cm and QR = 3.5 cm (all angles right angles).
(ii) On one line place the two sides end to end: a segment of 5 cm followed by 3.5 cm, total 8.5 cm.
(iii) Find the midpoint of the 8.5 cm segment and draw a semicircle on it as diameter.
(iv) At the junction point of the 5 cm and 3.5 cm parts, erect a perpendicular meeting the semicircle; this perpendicular is the side of the required square.
(v) Construct the square on this segment.
Justification:
The perpendicular from the junction point to the semicircle equals the geometric mean of the two parts: side = √(5 × 3.5) = √17.5 ≈ 4.18 cm. The square on it has area 17.5 cm², equal to the area of rectangle PQRS.

Q: Q3. Draw a triangle ABC such that mAB = 5 cm, mBC = 4 cm and mCA = 4.5 cm. Construct a rectangle equal in area to the given triangle.

Ans: Given:
△ABC with AB = 5 cm, BC = 4 cm and CA = 4.5 cm; if h is its altitude to BC, its area is (1/2) × 4 × h = 2h cm².
Required:
Draw △ABC and construct a rectangle equal in area to it.
Diagram: The finished figure is △ABC (base BC = 4 cm, CA = 4.5 cm, AB = 5 cm) with its altitude from A drawn and bisected, and a rectangle of length 4 cm and breadth h/2, equal in area to the triangle.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw BC = 4 cm; with centre B and radius 5 cm and centre C and radius 4.5 cm draw arcs meeting at A; join to complete △ABC.
(ii) Draw the altitude from A to BC and call its length h.
(iii) Bisect the altitude with the compass to obtain h/2.
(iv) Draw a segment equal to BC (4 cm); at its endpoints erect perpendiculars and mark h/2 on each.
(v) Join the tops to complete the rectangle.
Justification:
The rectangle has area BC × (h/2) = 4 × h/2 = 2h = (1/2) × BC × h, which is exactly the area of △ABC.

Q: Q4. Construct a square having area equal to the given rectangle.

Ans: Given:
A given rectangle (drawn in the unit) with length l and breadth b; its area is l × b.
Required:
Construct a square equal in area to the given rectangle.
Diagram: The finished figure is the given rectangle and a square whose side is the geometric mean of the rectangle's length and breadth, √(l × b).
Steps of Construction:
(i) Take the given rectangle with sides l and b.
(ii) On one line place the length l and the breadth b end to end.
(iii) Find the midpoint of the whole segment and draw a semicircle on it as diameter.
(iv) At the junction point of l and b, erect a perpendicular meeting the semicircle; this perpendicular is the side of the required square.
(v) Construct the square on this segment.
Justification:
The perpendicular to the diameter at the junction point equals the geometric mean of the two parts, √(l × b), so the square on it has area l × b, equal to the area of the given rectangle.

Q: Q5. Construct a square equal in area to a rectangle whose adjacent sides are 4.5 cm and 2.2 cm respectively. Measure the sides of the square and find its area and compare with the area of the rectangle.

Ans: Given:
A rectangle with adjacent sides 4.5 cm and 2.2 cm; its area is 4.5 × 2.2 = 9.9 cm².
Required:
Construct a square equal in area to the rectangle, measure its side, find its area and compare with the area of the rectangle.
Diagram: The finished figure is the 4.5 cm × 2.2 cm rectangle and a square whose measured side is about 3.15 cm, with area about 9.9 cm², the same as the rectangle.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the rectangle with sides 4.5 cm and 2.2 cm.
(ii) On one line place the two sides end to end: 4.5 cm followed by 2.2 cm, total 6.7 cm.
(iii) Find the midpoint of the 6.7 cm segment and draw a semicircle on it as diameter.
(iv) At the junction point erect a perpendicular meeting the semicircle; this perpendicular is the side of the required square.
(v) Construct the square on this segment and measure its side.
Justification:
The side of the square is the geometric mean √(4.5 × 2.2) = √9.9 ≈ 3.15 cm (by measurement about 3.1–3.2 cm). Its area is (3.15)² ≈ 9.9 cm², which equals the area of the rectangle, 4.5 × 2.2 = 9.9 cm². The two areas agree, as required.

Q: Q6. Construct a square equal in area to the sum of two squares having sides 3 cm and 4 cm respectively.

Ans: Given:
Two squares of sides 3 cm and 4 cm; their areas are 9 cm² and 16 cm², summing to 25 cm².
Required:
Construct a square whose area equals the sum of the areas of the two given squares.
Diagram: The finished figure shows the two squares of sides 3 cm and 4 cm, a right triangle with legs 3 cm and 4 cm and hypotenuse 5 cm, and the required square built on the 5 cm side.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the two squares with sides 3 cm and 4 cm.
(ii) Draw a right angle and mark 3 cm on one arm and 4 cm on the other.
(iii) Join the endpoints; the hypotenuse is the side of the required square.
(iv) Construct the square on the hypotenuse.
Justification:
By Pythagoras' theorem the hypotenuse is √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 cm. The square on it has area 25 cm² = 9 cm² + 16 cm², the sum of the areas of the two given squares.

Q: Q7. Construct a triangle having base 3.5 cm and other two sides equal to 3.4 cm and 3.8 cm respectively. Transform it into an equal square.

Ans: Given:
A triangle with base 3.5 cm and other sides 3.4 cm and 3.8 cm; if h is its altitude to the base, its area is (1/2) × 3.5 × h.
Required:
Construct the triangle and transform it into a square of equal area.
Diagram: The finished figure is the triangle (base 3.5 cm, sides 3.4 cm and 3.8 cm), the equal-area rectangle (length 3.5 cm, breadth h/2), and the square whose side is the geometric mean of 3.5 and h/2.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the base of 3.5 cm; with compass radii 3.4 cm and 3.8 cm from its endpoints draw arcs meeting at the third vertex; join to complete the triangle.
(ii) Draw the altitude h to the base and bisect it to get h/2.
(iii) Construct the rectangle equal in area to the triangle: length 3.5 cm, breadth h/2 (as in Q3).
(iv) Place 3.5 cm and h/2 end to end on a line, draw a semicircle on the whole as diameter, and erect a perpendicular at the junction point; this is the side of the required square.
(v) Construct the square on this segment.
Justification:
The rectangle has area 3.5 × (h/2) = (1/2) × 3.5 × h, equal to the triangle. The square's side is the geometric mean of the rectangle's sides, so its area equals the rectangle's area, and hence the triangle's area.

Q: Q8. Construct a triangle having base 5 cm and other sides equal to 5 cm and 6 cm. Also construct a square equal in area to the given triangle.

Ans: Given:
A triangle with base 5 cm and other sides 5 cm and 6 cm; if h is its altitude to the base, its area is (1/2) × 5 × h.
Required:
Construct the triangle and a square equal in area to it.
Diagram: The finished figure is the triangle (base 5 cm, sides 5 cm and 6 cm), the equal-area rectangle (length 5 cm, breadth h/2), and the square whose side is the geometric mean of 5 and h/2.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the base of 5 cm; with compass radii 5 cm and 6 cm from its endpoints draw arcs meeting at the third vertex; join to complete the triangle.
(ii) Draw the altitude h to the base and bisect it to get h/2.
(iii) Construct the rectangle equal in area to the triangle: length 5 cm, breadth h/2 (as in Q3).
(iv) Place 5 cm and h/2 end to end on a line, draw a semicircle on the whole as diameter, and erect a perpendicular at the junction point; this is the side of the required square.
(v) Construct the square on this segment.
Justification:
The rectangle has area 5 × (h/2) = (1/2) × 5 × h, equal to the triangle. The square's side is the geometric mean of the rectangle's sides, so its area equals the rectangle's area, and hence the triangle's area.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 17
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The first step in constructing an angle bisector is to place the compass point on the vertex and draw an arc cutting both arms of the angle.
  • Equal arcs drawn from both endpoints of a segment, crossing above and below it, joined by a line, give the perpendicular bisector of the segment.
  • A line segment joining the midpoint of one side of a triangle to its opposite vertex is called a median.
  • A line perpendicular to a segment at its midpoint is its perpendicular bisector; the perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcentre, which is equidistant from the vertices.
  • The bisectors of the angles of a triangle meet at the incentre, which is equidistant from the sides of the triangle; the altitudes are concurrent at the orthocentre.
  • The centroid divides each median in the ratio 2 : 1, and in an equilateral triangle the orthocentre, centroid and circumcentre are all the same point.
  • Knowing only the three angles of a triangle does not fix its size: infinitely many (similar) triangles can be constructed, so a side length is also needed for a unique triangle.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). What is the first step in constructing an angle bisector?

Options: (a) Draw a ray (b) Label the points of intersection (c) Measure the line (d) Place the compass point on the vertex

Correct answer: Place the compass point on the vertex

Q: Q1(ii). What geometric construction is shown in the diagram below? (The diagram shows a segment AB with two equal arcs drawn from A and from B crossing above and below the segment, and a dashed line joining the crossing points.)

Options: (a) A line parallel to a given line (b) An angle bisector (c) An angle congruent to a given angle (d) A perpendicular

Correct answer: A perpendicular

Q: Q1(iii). A line segment joining the midpoint of one side of a triangle to its opposite vertex is called

Options: (a) Perpendicular bisector (b) Median (c) Altitude (d) Angle bisector

Correct answer: Median

Q: Q1(iv). You are looking at a triangle whose orthocenter, centroid and circumcenter are all the same point. What type of triangle are you looking at?

Options: (a) Scalene (b) Isosceles (c) Equilateral (d) Right

Correct answer: Equilateral

Q: Q1(v). The centroid of a triangle divides the medians into the ratio of

Options: (a) 2 : 1 (b) 3 : 1 (c) 4 : 1 (d) 5 : 1

Correct answer: 2 : 1

Q: Q1(vi). A line which is perpendicular to a line segment at its mid-point is called a / an

Options: (a) Perpendicular bisector (b) Median (c) Altitude (d) Angle bisector

Correct answer: Perpendicular bisector

Q: Q1(vii). The point of intersection of the bisectors of the angles of a triangle is equidistant from the ________ of the triangle.

Options: (a) vertices (b) sides (c) altitudes (d) medians

Correct answer: sides

Q: Q1(viii). Altitudes of a triangle are ________.

Options: (a) equal in length (b) equidistant from the vertices (c) concurrent (d) perpendicular bisectors

Correct answer: concurrent

Q: Q1(ix). If measures of three angles of a triangle are known, how many triangles can be constructed?

Options: (a) Only one triangle (b) Two triangles (c) No triangle (d) Infinite triangles

Correct answer: Infinite triangles

Q: Q1(x). The point of intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle is equidistant from the ________ of the triangle.

Options: (a) altitudes (b) medians (c) sides (d) vertices

Correct answer: vertices

Q: Q2. Construct △ABC such that mAB = 3.7 cm, mBC = 2.5 cm and m∠B = 60°

Ans: Given:
mAB = 3.7 cm, mBC = 2.5 cm and m∠B = 60°; the angle at B is included between AB and BC.
Required:
Construct △ABC.
Diagram: The finished figure is △ABC with B at the left, BA = 3.7 cm and BC = 2.5 cm forming the 60° angle at B, A joined to C.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the line segment AB = 3.7 cm with the ruler.
(ii) At the vertex of the given angle, construct the angle of 60° at B.
(iii) Along the new arm, cut off BC = 2.5 cm with the compass.
(iv) Join the endpoints to complete the triangle and label all vertices and measures.
Justification:
Two sides and the included angle (S.A.S) determine a unique triangle.

Q: Q3. Construct a △ABC such that mBC = 5.8 cm, m∠A = 30° and m∠B = 45°

Ans: Given:
mBC = 5.8 cm, m∠A = 30° and m∠B = 45°; the third angle is m∠C = 180° − 30° − 45° = 105°, so the side BC has the angles 45° (at B) and 105° (at C) at its endpoints.
Required:
Construct △ABC.
Diagram: The finished figure is △ABC with base BC = 5.8 cm, A above the base where the 45° arm from B and the 105° arm from C meet (check: the angle at A measures 30°).
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the line segment BC = 5.8 cm with the ruler.
(ii) At its two endpoints, construct the angle of 45° at B and the angle of 105° at C (computed as 180° − 30° − 45°) on the same side of the segment.
(iii) Extend the two new arms until they meet at the third vertex.
(iv) Label all vertices and measures.
Justification:
The two given angles fix the third angle, so a side with its two endpoint angles (A.S.A) determines a unique triangle.

Q: Q4. Construct △ABC such that mAC = 4.5 cm, mBC = 4.1 cm and m∠B = 75°

Ans: Given:
mAC = 4.5 cm (the side opposite ∠B), mBC = 4.1 cm (a side adjacent to ∠B) and m∠B = 75° — the S.S.A case.
Required:
Construct △ABC.
Diagram: The finished figure is a single △ABC with B at the left, BC = 4.1 cm along the base, the 75° angle at B, and A on the 75° arm with AC = 4.5 cm, A joined to C.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw BC = 4.1 cm.
(ii) At B construct the angle of 75° and draw the arm (A lies on this arm).
(iii) The perpendicular distance from C to the arm is BC sin 75° ≈ 4.1 × 0.966 ≈ 3.96 cm; the given AC = 4.5 cm is greater than BC itself, so the arc of radius 4.5 cm centred at C cuts the arm in exactly one point, A.
(iv) Join A to C to complete the triangle.
Justification:
In the S.S.A case, when the side opposite the given angle (AC = 4.5 cm) is longer than the adjacent side (BC = 4.1 cm), the arc meets the arm in only one point, so exactly ONE triangle can be drawn.

Q: Q5. Construct △ABC, draw their angle bisectors and verify their concurrency: mAB = 5.3 cm, m∠A = 45° and m∠B = 45°

Ans: Given:
mAB = 5.3 cm, m∠A = 45° and m∠B = 45°; the side AB is included between the angles at A and B (the third angle at C is 90°).
Required:
Construct △ABC, draw the bisectors of its angles and verify that they are concurrent.
Diagram: The finished figure is △ABC with base AB = 5.3 cm, C above the base (right-angled at C); the bisectors from A, B and C meet at one interior point.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the line segment AB = 5.3 cm with the ruler.
(ii) At its two endpoints, construct the angle of 45° at A and the angle of 45° at B on the same side of the segment.
(iii) Extend the two new arms until they meet at the third vertex.
(iv) Label all vertices and measures.
(v) Draw the bisector of each angle: place the compass point on the vertex, draw an arc cutting both arms; from the two cutting points draw equal arcs meeting inside the angle; join the vertex to the meeting point.
(vi) The three bisectors are seen to meet at one point — their concurrency is verified.
Justification:
A side and its two adjacent angles (A.S.A) determine a unique triangle. Each bisector is drawn by the equal-arcs construction: the two small triangles formed on either side of the ray are congruent by S.S.S, so the ray halves the angle. The three angle bisectors of a triangle are concurrent (at the incentre), as verified in the figure.

Q: Q6. Construct △PQR, draw their altitudes and verify their concurrency: mPR = 5.8 cm, m∠P = 45° and m∠Q = 105°

Ans: Given:
mPR = 5.8 cm, m∠P = 45° and m∠Q = 105°; the third angle is m∠R = 180° − 45° − 105° = 30°, so the side PR has the angles 45° (at P) and 30° (at R) at its endpoints.
Required:
Construct △PQR, draw its altitudes and verify that they are concurrent.
Diagram: The finished figure is △PQR with base PR = 5.8 cm, Q above the base (check: the angle at Q measures 105°); the altitudes from P, Q and R are drawn, two of them falling on produced sides since the triangle is obtuse at Q, and their lines meet at one point.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the line segment PR = 5.8 cm with the ruler.
(ii) At its two endpoints, construct the angle of 45° at P and the angle of 30° at R (computed as 180° − 45° − 105°) on the same side of the segment.
(iii) Extend the two new arms until they meet at the third vertex.
(iv) Label all vertices and measures.
(v) Draw the altitude from each vertex: place the compass point on the vertex, draw an arc cutting the opposite side (produced if necessary) at two points; from these points draw equal arcs meeting beyond the side; join the vertex to the meeting point — the line is perpendicular to the opposite side.
(vi) The three altitudes are seen to meet at one point — their concurrency is verified.
Justification:
The two given angles fix the third angle, so a side with its two endpoint angles (A.S.A) determines a unique triangle. Each altitude is drawn by the perpendicular-from-a-point construction, so it is perpendicular to the opposite side. The three altitudes of a triangle are concurrent (at the orthocentre), as verified in the figure.

Q: Q7. Construct △UVW, draw their perpendicular bisectors and verify their concurrency: mUW = 5.8 cm, m∠U = 45° and m∠V = 105°

Ans: Given:
mUW = 5.8 cm, m∠U = 45° and m∠V = 105°; the third angle is m∠W = 180° − 45° − 105° = 30°, so the side UW has the angles 45° (at U) and 30° (at W) at its endpoints.
Required:
Construct △UVW, draw the perpendicular bisectors of its sides and verify that they are concurrent.
Diagram: The finished figure is △UVW with base UW = 5.8 cm, V above the base (check: the angle at V measures 105°); the perpendicular bisectors of the three sides meet at one point.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the line segment UW = 5.8 cm with the ruler.
(ii) At its two endpoints, construct the angle of 45° at U and the angle of 30° at W (computed as 180° − 45° − 105°) on the same side of the segment.
(iii) Extend the two new arms until they meet at the third vertex.
(iv) Label all vertices and measures.
(v) Draw the perpendicular bisector of each side: with radius more than half the side, draw arcs above and below the side from both endpoints; join the two meeting points of the arcs.
(vi) The three perpendicular bisectors are seen to meet at one point — their concurrency is verified.
Justification:
The two given angles fix the third angle, so a side with its two endpoint angles (A.S.A) determines a unique triangle. Each perpendicular bisector is drawn by equal arcs from the endpoints of a side; every point on it is equidistant from the side's endpoints. The three perpendicular bisectors of a triangle are concurrent (at the circumcentre), as verified in the figure.

Q: Q8. Construct △XYZ, draw their medians and verify their concurrency: mZX = 6 cm, m∠Y = 60° and m∠Z = 75°

Ans: Given:
mZX = 6 cm, m∠Y = 60° and m∠Z = 75°; the third angle is m∠X = 180° − 60° − 75° = 45°, so the side ZX has the angles 75° (at Z) and 45° (at X) at its endpoints.
Required:
Construct △XYZ, draw its medians and verify that they are concurrent.
Diagram: The finished figure is △XYZ with base ZX = 6 cm, Y above the base; the medians from X, Y and Z to the midpoints of the opposite sides meet at one interior point.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the line segment ZX = 6 cm with the ruler.
(ii) At its two endpoints, construct the angle of 75° at Z and the angle of 45° at X (computed as 180° − 60° − 75°) on the same side of the segment.
(iii) Extend the two new arms until they meet at the third vertex.
(iv) Label all vertices and measures.
(v) Find the midpoint of each side with the compass (arcs from both endpoints, as for a perpendicular bisector) and join it to the opposite vertex to draw the three medians.
(vi) The three medians are seen to meet at one point — their concurrency is verified.
Justification:
The two given angles fix the third angle, so a side with its two endpoint angles (A.S.A) determines a unique triangle. Each median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side, the midpoint being found by the compass bisection construction. The three medians of a triangle are concurrent (at the centroid), as verified in the figure.

Q: Q9. Draw a triangle PQR such that mPQ = 5.6 cm, mQR = 4.5 cm and mRP = 3.4 cm. Construct a triangle SPQ equivalent in area to the triangle PQR.

Ans: Given:
△PQR with PQ = 5.6 cm, QR = 4.5 cm and RP = 3.4 cm (the three sides).
Required:
Draw △PQR and construct △SPQ, on the same base PQ, equivalent (equal) in area to △PQR.
Diagram: The finished figure is △PQR with base PQ = 5.6 cm and R above it, a line through R parallel to PQ, and a point S taken on that line with S joined to P and Q, forming △SPQ.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw PQ = 5.6 cm; with centre P and radius RP = 3.4 cm and centre Q and radius QR = 4.5 cm draw arcs meeting at R; join to complete △PQR.
(ii) Through R draw a line parallel to PQ (copy the angle at P or Q to make corresponding angles equal).
(iii) Take any point S on this parallel line.
(iv) Join S to P and S to Q; △SPQ is the required triangle.
Justification:
△SPQ and △PQR stand on the same base PQ and between the same parallels (PQ and the line through R and S), so they have the same altitude and are equal in area. Any point S on the parallel gives such a triangle.

Q: Q10. Construct a rectangle whose adjacent sides are 2.5 cm and 5 cm respectively. Transform it into an equal square.

Ans: Given:
A rectangle with adjacent sides 2.5 cm and 5 cm; its area is 2.5 × 5 = 12.5 cm².
Required:
Construct the rectangle and transform it into a square of equal area.
Diagram: The finished figure is the rectangle (2.5 cm by 5 cm) and a square of side √12.5 ≈ 3.54 cm, whose area is 12.5 cm².
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the rectangle with adjacent sides 2.5 cm and 5 cm (all angles right angles).
(ii) On one line place the two sides end to end: 5 cm followed by 2.5 cm, total 7.5 cm.
(iii) Find the midpoint of the 7.5 cm segment and draw a semicircle on it as diameter.
(iv) At the junction point erect a perpendicular meeting the semicircle; this perpendicular is the side of the required square.
(v) Construct the square on this segment.
Justification:
The perpendicular to the diameter at the junction point equals the geometric mean of the two parts: side = √(5 × 2.5) = √12.5 ≈ 3.54 cm. The square on it has area 12.5 cm², equal to the area of the rectangle.

mcqs.q: What is the first step in constructing an angle bisector?
options: Place the compass point on the vertex
mcqs.why: The angle bisector construction begins by placing the compass point on the vertex of the angle and drawing an arc that cuts both arms. The two cutting points are then used for the equal arcs that fix the bisector ray.

mcqs.q: A segment AB has two equal arcs drawn from A and from B crossing above and below the segment, and the crossing points are joined by a dashed line. What construction is this?
options: A line parallel to a given line
An angle congruent to a given angle
mcqs.why: Equal arcs from both endpoints of a segment, intersecting above and below, is the standard construction of the perpendicular bisector: the joining line is perpendicular to AB at its midpoint, and every point on it is equidistant from A and B.

mcqs.q: A line segment joining the midpoint of one side of a triangle to its opposite vertex is called a:
mcqs.why: By definition, a median joins a vertex of a triangle to the midpoint of the opposite side. This is the line drawn in the median constructions of Exercise 17.2, and the three medians meet at the centroid.

mcqs.q: You are looking at a triangle whose orthocentre, centroid and circumcentre are all the same point. What type of triangle is it?
mcqs.why: Only in an equilateral triangle do the altitudes, medians and perpendicular bisectors all coincide, so the orthocentre, centroid and circumcentre fall at one and the same central point.

mcqs.q: The centroid of a triangle divides each median in the ratio:
mcqs.why: The centroid, where the three medians meet, divides each median in the ratio 2 : 1, the longer part being from the vertex to the centroid and the shorter part from the centroid to the midpoint of the side.

mcqs.q: A line which is perpendicular to a line segment at its midpoint is called a/an:
mcqs.why: A line that cuts a segment at its midpoint and is perpendicular to it is by definition the perpendicular bisector of that segment. It is constructed with equal arcs from the two endpoints of the segment.

mcqs.q: The point of intersection of the bisectors of the angles of a triangle is equidistant from the ________ of the triangle.
mcqs.why: The angle bisectors meet at the incentre. Every point on an angle bisector is equidistant from the two sides forming the angle, so the incentre is equidistant from all three sides of the triangle.

mcqs.q: The altitudes of a triangle are ________.
mcqs.why: The three altitudes of a triangle always meet in a single point, the orthocentre, so they are concurrent. They are not generally equal in length, and an altitude is not a perpendicular bisector unless the triangle is isosceles at that vertex.

mcqs.q: If the measures of the three angles of a triangle are known, how many triangles can be constructed?
mcqs.why: Three angles fix only the shape, not the size: any scale gives a similar triangle with the same three angles. Without at least one side length, infinitely many triangles can be constructed.

mcqs.q: The point of intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle is equidistant from the ________ of the triangle.
mcqs.why: The perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcentre. Every point on the perpendicular bisector of a side is equidistant from that side's two endpoints, so the circumcentre is equidistant from all three vertices of the triangle.
